title: Victoria Beckham's company makes its first profit after 18 years
author: Ian Youngs
content:
![Victoria Beckham head and shoulders, looking to one side with a hand on the collar of a cream jacket, in front of a display of cream roses](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/6918/live/636dc020-a55b-11f1-9acf-19576105f049.jpg)
- Published
Victoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has made an operating profit for the first time since she founded it in 2008, the company has said.
Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd, which is led by the former Spice Girl as creative director, made an operating profit of Â£7.3m in 2025, accounts show, after years of losses.
"We have all worked hard for a long time for this moment of profitability and growth," Lady Beckham told the Financial Times, external.
"We've been very transparent about the problems that we had in the business but have recovered and are now growing at a sensible pace. After 20 years, people don't look at my brand as a celebrity brand any more."
Skincare success
Last year, a Netflix documentary told the story of her attempting to establish a fashion brand and achieve profitability - and the series itself helped boost sales, "with particularly strong momentum in denim and jersey", according to the accounts.
The fashion side of the company delivered "strong double-digit growth" overall in 2025, they said, while the beauty side, which launched in 2019, "delivered one of its strongest performances to date".
That was led by the popularity of her Foundation Drops, which had a 25,000-strong waiting list and which doubled the size of the skincare part of the company.
![Victoria Beckham standing and smiling in front of a catwalk audience at Victoria Beckham Ready To Wear Spring 2024 on September 29, 2023 in Paris](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/a2eb/live/d9afcc60-a55b-11f1-9acf-19576105f049.jpg)
Victoria Beckham on the catwalk at one of her brand's fashion shows in Paris in 2023
The Netflix documentary showed the former pop star talking about her attempts to overcome doubters to be taken seriously as a designer and entrepreneur, then running into financial trouble when the company was "tens of millions in the red".
The business was bailed out by her husband Sir David, who told the programme: "For her to have to come to me and say, 'Can I have some... We need some more money, the business needs more money' - that was hard for both of us because I didn't have the money to keep doing this."
Lady Beckham said: "If he hadn't believed in me I wouldn't still have a business now."
She went on to get Â£30m investment by selling 30% of the company to NEO Investment Partners in 2017, who launched a restructure.
'Significant milestone'
That included tackling what Beckham admitted was "mindblowing" waste, including "flying chairs from one side of the world to another" and spending what NEO's David Belhassen said was "70,000 a year" on office plants.
In a statement on Monday, Belhassen, who is chairman of Victoria Beckham Holdings, said: "With two complementary growth engines in fashion and beauty, an increasingly international customer base and a focused operating model, the business is powerfully positioned for its next phase of profitable growth."
CEO Sybille DarricarrÃ¨re Lunel said: "Achieving our first operating profit is a landmark moment for Victoria Beckham and reflects several years of disciplined execution and strategic investment.
"Delivering this result against a more challenging luxury market and macro backdrop makes it an even more significant milestone for the business."
summary: Victoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has achieved its first-ever operating profit of £7.3m in 2025 after years of previous losses. The milestone follows strategic restructuring, investment, and boosted sales driven by both strong product performance—such as skincare and denim—and a recent Netflix documentary. The company previously faced significant financial difficulties and waste before being supported by outside investment and management changes.
key_points: Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd reported an operating profit of £7.3m in 2025, marking its first profitability since founding in 2008.
A recent Netflix documentary and strong momentum in denim, jersey, and beauty products helped boost sales.
The skincare line grew significantly, largely driven by the popularity of Foundation Drops which had a 25,000-strong waiting list.
The business underwent restructuring and cost-cutting measures after receiving a £30m investment from NEO Investment Partners in 2017.

title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20
author: Ruth Comerford
content:
![An investor looks at an electronic board showing stock information with numbers highlighted in red and lime green against a black background. The investor has her back to the camera and has her left hand resting on her head.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/0b34/live/537541c0-a556-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.
Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.
Addressing finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".
Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.
Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.
"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.
Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".
Bailey, who is also chairman of the Financial Stability Board watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.
His warning comes several months after UK Chancellor John Healey announced a Â£100m fund aimed at backing British AI start-ups.
That is part of the government's efforts to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.
Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.
A UK government spokesperson said its' new AI economics institute was working with international partners to build "a stronger shared understanding of how AI is transforming economies around the world."
"The institute is the first government-backed body of its kind focused on AI's economic impact, helping policymakers understand what AI means for growth, productivity, jobs and public services as the technology develops at pace," the spokesperson said.
But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.
![Andrew Bailey, Bank of England governor, talking at a press conference after the Bank cut interest rates on 7th November](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/6933/live/a6f195b0-a292-11ef-b8c0-b996e628df5a.jpg)
This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.
The FSB which Bailey leads is a global watchdog which monitors finance ministry officials, banks and securities regulators. It includes officials from the US, UK, France, Germany, Canada, Japan, Australia, China and Saudi Arabia.
summary: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could trigger a global economic downturn and create major cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Speaking in the US, Bailey highlighted risks stemming from high stock valuations, increased investor borrowing, and market concentration within a few major tech companies. He urged financial security leaders to develop steps for safe model deployment and warned that firms must prepare for simultaneous security breaches.
key_points: Andrew Bailey warned G20 ministers that an AI sector collapse could cause a worldwide market correction.
High stock valuations, increased leverage, and market concentration threaten to amplify future financial downturns.
Major tech companies and AI models are increasingly capable of bypassing banking and financial center safeguards.
The UK government has established an AI economics institute to understand the technology's impact on growth and productivity.

title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England governor tells G20
author: Simon Goodley
content:
The Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, has joined the throng of figures warning about the global risks posed by the most advanced artificial intelligence technology.
In a two-page letter sent to international finance ministers and central bank governors as part of his role as chair of the international Financial Stability Board (FSB), Bailey said “frontier” AI models were “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities”.
He said the models risked destabilising the “highly interconnected” global financial system via cyber-disruption that “can spread across jurisdictions”.
Bailey wrote to G20 finance ministers and central bank governors before their meeting in North Carolina, US, this week: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols in place to manage the development, release, and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond”.
His letter adds to alarm bells about AI that have been sounded by prominent technologists over the past few weeks – and mirrors his previous calls for international cooperation to tackle growing AI threats, when he told City bosses: “No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.”
![An illustration showing a series of bubbles, one marked AI bubble, set over a circuit board](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4a514c062129c0c284efe3e1a45a4c91b7323bdb/728_0_6880_5504/master/6880.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Last month, a letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind – also shone a light on the concerns of the engineers working on the technology every day.
It stated: “There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems,” before going on to ask for the US government’s support for “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.
Earlier this month, it also emerged that OpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its cutting-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm.
Extending this theme into the world of financial policy, Bailey continued: “For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber-risk. Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber-risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers.”
Bailey called on those tasked with safeguarding the world’s financial systems to prioritise “appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis”.
after newsletter promotion
The letter also noted Bailey’s concerns about the increased use of leverage in bond and equity markets, which he said was combining with high valuations in concentrated financial markets – particularly fuelled by investor optimism about the prospects of AI – in a way that could amplify a future market correction.
“I remain concerned therefore that a large shock or combination of shocks could concurrently trigger multiple vulnerabilities,” Bailey wrote.
Bailey has been governor of the Bank of England since March 2020, and previously headed both the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority, the UK’s two main financial regulators. He was appointed chair of the FSB last year.
The FSB, based in Basel, Switzerland, coordinates the work at international level of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies in an effort to develop effective regulation and policies in the interest of financial stability.
summary: Bank of England governor and Financial Stability Board chair Andrew Bailey warned G20 finance ministers that advanced artificial intelligence could trigger a global economic downturn. In a letter ahead of the G20 meeting, Bailey highlighted risks such as cross-border cyber-disruption, inadequate regulatory protocols, and market vulnerabilities amplified by AI-driven investor optimism. He urged international policymakers to prioritize safe and responsible AI deployment to protect financial stability.
key_points: Andrew Bailey warned international finance leaders that advanced 'frontier' AI models pose significant risks to the global financial system.
The governor highlighted that many jurisdictions lack the protocols needed to manage the deployment of advanced AI models.
A primary financial concern is AI's potential to alter cyber-risk, threatening market confidence through widespread disruption.
Bailey noted that high market valuations fueled by AI optimism could amplify a future market correction if triggered by a shock.

title: Renters blocked from installing £600 plug-in solar panels
author: Adam Forrest
content:
Landlords could block tenants from using plug-in solar panel kits because of “messy minefield” around planning rules, The i Paper has been told.
Labour ministers have been urged to create a clear legal framework for both landlords and renters so tenants can cut their energy bills by up to £110 a year.
The first self-install solar kits went on sale last week for £699, after the Government created new product compliance rules.
Prices are expected to drop to under £600 as more retailers start stocking the home renewables devices. One kit should be available for £599 in October.
The first compliant plug-in solar kits by British firm UKsol are designed to be set up in gardens, rather than clipped onto balconies.
Balcony products are expected to go on sale soon, aimed at flat-dwelling renters who have struggled to benefit from traditional rooftop solar. However, one leading housing association has already blocked tenants from installing them.
Ministers want landlords to approve requests
The Government has made it clear that decisions on whether to approve tenants’ requests to use plug-in solar are still ultimately a matter for landlords.
Ministers have written to the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) making it clear that they expect the new solar kits to be looked on “favourably”.
Climate minister Katie White said earlier this year that the Government could “consider” changes to the law if plug-in becomes a “friction” point between tenants and landlords.
But having changed regulations to allow the products to be sold, energy minister Martin McCluskey suggested last week that he didn’t think further legislation would be necessary.
“I don’t see a reason why a landlord should needlessly withdraw consent or not provide consent,” he told reporters.
![Climate minister Katie White visiting UKSOL factory to see new plug-in solar kits (Photo: DESNZ)](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309678840.jpg?w=644)
However, the NRLA told The i Paper that there was no clear guidance for landlords on the regulatory issues.
“There is no clear guidance for landlords who have a duty to ensure their properties remain safe and free from hazards,” said the NRLA’s Meera Chindooroy.
“The Government should publish this as soon as possible to support conversations between tenants and landlords,” the deputy director of campaigns added.
Landlords will cite insurance fears to say ‘no’
Rule changes which came into force on 27 August mean plug-in solar kits are “permitted development” which do not generally require planning consent.
But there are a series of exceptions. Plug-in panels will need planning permission if they’re installed “on a wooden wall, balcony or enclosure or on any part of the exterior of a block of flats which is clad in timber”.
There are also a series of detailed “protrusion” limits – including rules that stop panels “protruding more than 0.4 metres beyond the plane of the wall” – if tenants and landlords want to avoid the need for planning permission.
Justin Dring, an expert at Independent Solar Consultants, who advises property owners, thinks many landlords could still say “no” to plug-in solar panels.
Landlords will “cite insurance concerns”, he said. Their fears are based on uncertainty over whether tenants will install the devices safely, or will install them a way that doesn’t meet planning rules.
“I could see landlords saying, ‘You’re not plugging that in in my property,'” Dring told The i Paper.
“When it comes to insurance, the liability question if a panel is dislodged in a storm, or damages a neighbour’s property, or causes an electrical fault, is genuinely unresolved territory.”
“It’s a really cloudy, messy situation – it’s a minefield,” said Dring. “For tenants and landlords, if things go wrong there may be fingers pointed in every direction.”
Dring added: “It would be better [for the Government] to set out the regulations and what requires planning permission much more clearly.”
![ERFURT, GERMANY - SEPTEMBER 01: Solar energy panels hang from a residential apartment balcony on September 01, 2024 in Erfurt, Germany. Many people in Germany have taken advantage of falling prices for solar panels combined with a government subsidy and eased German regulations to install solar energy panels on their balconies for home electricity production. (Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images)](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/SEI_290865004_7db051.jpg?w=644)
Paul Shamplina, founder of Landlord Action, said the Government should set out planning guidance “more much clearly” using “practical layman’s language”.
Most landlords “will want to help their tenants save money, so hopefully there’s no issue in most cases, if tenants can explain clearly how it’s safe”, said Shamplina.
However, he warned that some landlords may well refuse tenants’ request. They might not want “the headache and hassle of working out if they need planning permission”, he said. “They might have insurance concerns, because they have enough risk on their plate.”
Germany’s legal change to boost tenants’ rights
The German government changed the law to make it difficult for landlords to refuse tenants’ permission for plug-in solar.
But Shamplina urged Labour not to bring in more renters’ rights legislation in the UK.
“If the guidance is made clear, there’s no need to legislate. Legislation would only cause more strain on an industry that is suffocating.”
Wider uptake of plug-in solar among tenants in flats may depend on whether social housing providers allow the technology.
One leading housing association, Sovereign Network Group – which manages 86,000 homes in England – has already banned its tenants from installing plug-in panels.
“We’re not permitting customers to install plug-in or plug-and-play solar panels in the homes we manage,” said Alexia Evans, SNG’s chief people and transformation officer. She said plug-in systems “present electrical safety risks and may not be appropriate for every home”.
The Government has said an independent electrical safety study had already concluded that plug-in solar panels were safe, provided products were compliant.
Wickes said it will start selling plug-in solar kits “in the coming weeks”. Currys, Lidl, Asda, B&Q, Screwfix and Amazon are also expected to make products available.
Labour’s Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said plug-in solar was “a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills”.
summary: Renters in the UK face potential blocks from landlords in using new plug-in solar panel kits due to complex planning rules and liability concerns. While the government expects landlords to look favorably upon requests to help tenants cut energy bills, industry experts warn that insurance fears and unclear regulations may lead to widespread rejections. Some housing associations have already banned the technology over electrical safety and property suitability risks.
key_points: New self-install plug-in solar kits recently went on sale for under £700, with prices expected to drop below £600.
The National Residential Landlords Association and property experts have warned that planning rules and insurance liability regarding the panels remain a messy minefield.
Decisions on whether to approve tenants' requests to use plug-in solar are ultimately up to landlords.
At least one major housing association, Sovereign Network Group, has already banned tenants from installing the panels due to safety and suitability risks.

title: Meta may be $18bn poorer, but it is still the real winner
author: Janet Daley
content:
![Mark Zuckerberg](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000481639897_17880135938280_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLfZdHPP_Jms68Nei_IBhruk42DQBkRg40hW7ifiDKAM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Mark Zuckerberg](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000481639897_17880135938280_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqLfZdHPP_Jms68Nei_IBhruk42DQBkRg40hW7ifiDKAM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Everybody is saying that this was social media’s “big tobacco” moment: the historic point at which an industry had to face up to its responsibilities and stop ignoring the damage that its product was causing. But is big social media doing any of this? They have not, in fact, acknowledged that they are in any way to blame.
Social media algorithms are not opioids. But what happened in the Meta case had the potential of being (but wasn’t in the end) the industry’s “big opioid” moment. There are echoes of the scandal in which the Purdue pharmaceutical company, owned by the Sackler family, was found to be culpable of marketing a pain-killing product that produced addiction so severe that it could result in death.
The Meta settlement, unlike the Purdue Pharma story, has not ended with the disgrace of the company and its founders – or indeed a finding of culpability. Where the Sackler name fell into such disrepute that it had to be removed from the art galleries which the family had donated to public museums, the founders of Meta walked from the court in California with their pride – and their empires – largely intact.
The conclusion – if it can be called that – of the legal action against them seemed bizarrely contradictory. Mark Zuckerberg agreed for Meta – if other social-media firms agree to similar arrangements and restrictions – to hand over $18bn as a settlement to US state governments and territories including those which had not been directly involved in the suit. (This sounds like a vast fortune but in terms of his own wealth and Meta’s share price, it is peanuts.)
The curious thing about this settlement in the terms of ordinary human logic as opposed to acceptable legal procedure, is that the company was offering this seemingly vast sum of money even though it did not admit any liability. In other words – again to put it in normal human language – the company is saying, we are prepared to pay up but not accept the blame.
And at the same time, Meta has also agreed to amend – but not entirely remove – those features of its media such as infinite scroll, autoplay and algorithmic recommendations which had been cited as particularly dangerous to children because of their addictive properties. These will now be time limited and turned off at the times of day and night when children were thought to be most vulnerable.
So let’s get this straight. Meta admits no liability – in other words, claims that the things they were doing were not harmful or dangerous. But anyway, they promise that they won’t do them any more.
Or at least, they will modify them so that they won’t be – what? Harmful and dangerous? No, that can’t be right because the defence argument was that they were never harmful or dangerous. So what exactly has been proved – or not proved – here?
The attorneys general of those states that brought the action wanted to establish that Meta was marketing a product that was deliberately designed to be addictive. This would have made the Sackler analogy particularly apt. It was that explicit claim about motive that Meta was determined to defeat because it would have implied criminal liability and Sackler-level disgrace. So the Zuckerberg defence won the argument that mattered most to their survival.
![Purdue Pharma logo at its offices in Stamford, Conn](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000209309219_17880143237150_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
They would pay out money in compensation and amend some of their practices out of the goodness of their hearts and to show contrition for any damage caused – even though none of it was their fault. It was critical that they distinguish their product – which they believed could be used safely much of the time – from an opioid which would inevitably cause addiction.
And they succeeded. The settlement appears to have been accepted without challenge. So however much money they pay out and whatever minor tweaks they may make to their products, they won this case.
There is a particular line of defence of Meta’s position taken up and endlessly repeated by apparently conscientious parties which really needs to be addressed. That is that whatever potential endangerment the Meta sites may have presented to children, it was the responsibility of their parents to prevent the excessive exposure that might have caused the damage. It was not the moral duty of the social media company to protect everybody’s children.
I wonder whether the people who argue this way would apply the same principle to, say, the sale of alcohol? Should we remove the minimum age limit for buying beer in a pub, or liquor from a supermarket because it is up to parents to see to it that their 10-year-olds do not purchase alcohol?
Concern for the welfare of children is not a purely private matter. We do not regard their safety as nobody’s business outside their own immediate family. If that were so, the law would not be able to intervene to prevent parents from abusing their children. The state does assume the right to remove children from dangerous circumstances in their familial homes because children are considered to be everybody’s business. There is something deeply embedded in human conscience, perhaps for hard evolutionary reasons, that decrees that the young must be protected by the whole community.
So can we shut down this rather nasty insinuation that children cannot be harmed by any agency or force if their parents are sufficiently caring? As if bereaved or distraught families had only themselves to blame for the sinister, insidious influence of enterprises which create devices designed to captivate and hold attention, whatever the consequences?
But this is not just about children. The most insidious aspect of this farrago is the assumption that the amorality of social media is only a risk to the immature and vulnerable.
Companies like Meta created the template for what is now the prevailing defence of these hugely powerful forces. Unlike any of the established media forms, they accept only very limited responsibility – legal or ethical – for their content. They insist that they cannot be susceptible to any governmental limits or national jurisdictions because, not being “publishers” in the traditional sense, they do not control what appears on their sites.
They are, in other words, lawless and beyond the reach of democratic accountability. This might be one of the worst examples of power without responsibility that the modern world has faced.
summary: Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement with US state governments without admitting any liability or criminal culpability regarding the addictiveness of its platforms. As part of the arrangement, the company will time-limit features like infinite scroll and algorithmic recommendations for children, while successfully avoiding the disgrace and liability faced by pharmaceutical companies in similar scandals. Despite the financial payout and product modifications, Meta maintains that it is not responsible for platform content or parental supervision duties.
key_points: Meta agreed to pay an $18 billion settlement to US state governments and territories without admitting any liability.
The company will modify features like infinite scroll and algorithmic recommendations to be time-limited for children at vulnerable hours.
Meta successfully avoided a ruling of criminal culpability and preserved the reputations of its founders, distinguishing its outcome from the Purdue Pharma scandal.
The article criticizes the defense argument that parents alone bear the responsibility for protecting children from addictive social media products.

title: 'Cowboy builders' targeted in new government clampdown
author: Emer Moreau
content:
![A couple looks at plans with a builder in their home, which is under renovation](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/3e64/live/5cd9a9c0-a22e-11f1-bd54-531a21306a62.jpg)
The prime minister said rogue builders gave "decent, hardworking" traders a bad name [file pic]
- Published
People carrying out home renovations will gain greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards, the government has said.
Traders signing up to the scheme launching next month will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.
The National Federation of Builders said the changes would not stop rogue operators while the Tories suggested there would be added paperwork for firms already operating legitimately.
Citizens Advice has said home renovations are one of its biggest sources of consumer complaints.
The government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months have experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.
It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority, external suggesting customers lost more Â£10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.
BBC News has previously reported on "bait-and-switch" locksmith scams, where customers were given an initial cheap quote before hidden charges and unnecessary work were added.
Under the new traders' scheme, customers' money will be held in an account and released in parts after certain milestones in projects are completed.
'Decent, hardworking' traders given bad name
The National Federation of Builders (NFB) told BBC Breakfast there are already schemes in place to find trustworthy builders.
Adas Rico Wojtulewicz-Richmond, the NFB's director of policy, said: "Is this scheme going to stop bad actors operating and ripping people off? I don't think it will."
He said a better approach would be for every project to have a "passport" which records all the work done.
"It protects consumers because you can find out which companies are doing a poor job, and it brings up the industry standards," he said.
The Chartered Trading Standards Institute (CTSI) said the new scheme would clamp down on rogue traders "who take the money and run", but urged the government to go further to protect vulnerable people from shoddy works and repairs.
John Herriman, CTSI's chief executive, said government funding schemes like the Warm Homes Plan, external could create opportunities for fraudulent traders.
"CTSI would therefore urge the government to see this as a great first step and to introduce a mandatory licence for tradespeople working in the home repair and maintenance sector, which would make it simpler and cheaper for enforcement agencies â including Trading Standards â to prosecute fraudulent tradespeople," he said.
BBC News has previously reported on botched insulation jobs carried out through government schemes since 2022.
Major defects have been found in over 30,000 houses linked to the schemes.
The prime minister said rogue tradespeople gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and would be "putting the cowboys out of business".
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said that, while home improvements can be stressful, "we're taking action to protect consumers, support reputable traders and make sure people can spend their money with greater confidence and security".
Shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith said the announcement looks like "the sort of government initiative that risks the unintended consequence of piling more paperwork onto the majority of businesses who already do the right thing".
He said: "The government would do far better to beef up law enforcement and have tougher sentences for the minority who fraudulently rip off customers. Those who break the rules will keep breaking them regardless of whether there is an app in the way."
Liberal Democrat business spokesperson Sarah Olney said: "Rogue builders cause real harm and ruin real lives every year. The current system is simply not fit for purpose and this half-baked announcement falls frustratingly short from fixing it.
"A voluntary code for tradespeople completely misses the mark. Rogue operators won't voluntarily sign up - they will simply keep exploiting families in the shadows."
Clampdown on 'intimidating' bailiffs
Alongside action on rogue tradespeople, the government has announced plans to regulate private bailiffs in England and Wales, to protect people in debt from "intimidating behaviour, unfair treatment or being pushed into excessive repayment arrangements".
Under the changes, people facing enforcement action will have access to an independent complaints process, and private bailiffs will be held to professional standards.
Sarah Sackman, minister for courts and legal services, said bailiffs did an important job, but "with that responsibility must come high standards".
As part of the changes, the government will look at how organisations such as Trading Standards work with regulators and enforcement bodies "so consumers are not passed from pillar to post".
Last year, a Freedom of Information request by Which? revealed that understaffing in trading standards teams was leading to more scams and dangerous products being sold.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/2528/live/73698360-a2ae-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
summary: The UK government has announced a new clampdown on rogue builders and private bailiffs to increase consumer protections and set higher professional standards. The initiative includes a trusted traders database and a phased payment system where funds are released after project milestones are met. While some officials and consumer groups welcomed the measures as a positive first step, critics and trade bodies argued the plan does not go far enough or risks adding unnecessary paperwork for legitimate businesses.
key_points: A new government scheme launching next month will introduce a database of trusted traders and a secure payment system that releases funds in milestones.
Data cited by the government indicates over a quarter of people carrying out home improvements in the past 18 months experienced problems with builders.
The National Federation of Builders and the Liberal Democrats criticized the plan as insufficient, arguing that rogue operators will not voluntarily sign up.
The Chartered Trading Standards Institute urged the government to introduce a mandatory licence for tradespeople to better prosecute fraudsters.
The government has also announced plans to regulate private bailiffs in England and Wales to prevent intimidating behaviour and provide an independent complaints process.

title: ‘Without us, no wheel would turn’: the unsung heroes keeping England’s transport moving
author: Gwyn Topham
content:
Not many people get to park their car here – bang in the middle of Heathrow airport, on the taxiway just a stretch of grass away from where a line of passenger planes is coming in to land.
It’s close enough to see the shimmering air and smoke as nose tyres hit the tarmac. “An A380 will put down as much rubber as a car’s entire tyre,” Jack Quantick-Thorne says. He knows – part of his job is to ensure the runway team scrapes it off and patches things up overnight. And it is all recycled, he adds.
The airfield operations officer is not in the limelight much, but is one of a host of unsung workers keeping transport moving. And some jobs far from the public eye turn out to be not only essential, but surprisingly challenging.
Jack Quantick-Thorne, airfield operations officer, Heathrow
Passengers might only catch a glimpse of Quantick-Thorne from a window seat on landing, if he grabs the paddles to marshal a plane into the exact designated spot at the stand. “People just think you’re that person with the table tennis bats,” he grimaces slightly, as the Guardian requests a demonstration. “That’s like 5% of my job.”
In fact, most planes are now brought to the stand via laser-guided electronic displays. But human marshalling remains a crucial backup. Brandishing the paddles, Quantick-Thorne beckons in a taxiing British Airways arrival, the pilot peering down from the cockpit and steering 50 tonnes of plane straight towards him. The nosewheel travels bang on the guideline, stopping exactly in position for the airbridge to swing in and allow passengers to disembark.
Nerve-racking? “No. When you’ve got a really big plane, an A380, you need a second marshal right by the wheel to check it’s stopped in the right place,” he says.
Back in the car, the job continues: “I’m patrolling, I’m looking around, scanning everything – is the refueller doing his job properly, has the aircraft got chocks under its wheels?”
That includes monitoring the road system under Heathrow’s airfields, recognising every vehicle and checking any infringement: drivers here can also clock up points on their licence, if he spots them.
Officers also need to look out for wildlife – particularly birds, a serious danger for jet planes (and vice versa). How does he deal with them? “We’ve got methods of dispersal,” says the airfield operations officer.
These, marvellously, turn out to be speakers on the roof of the van, which play a range of bird sounds: “If I saw a flock of starlings, if I played a starling noise, the starling would think, ‘Oh, maybe there’s a predator nearby,’ and they fly off.”
And, he demonstrates, “I’ve got common gull. Black-headed gull. I’ve got a falcon”.
Are there falcons? “No,” he explains patiently. “So you think about it from a bird’s point of view. If there’s a pigeon over there, best play a falcon so it will fly off.”
![Jack Quantick-Thorne stands with his back to the camera directing planes with his paddles.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c1aa272453f7c045a6122b7cbed7ffc4ee8df653/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
If he now knows birds, it’s the planes that drew him here. He was previously at Nats, the air traffic control centre in Swanwick, managing the planes, but never up close. There is more to it than the paddles – but, he confesses, he takes every opportunity to use them, and records each plane that he has marshalled, including every aircraft in BA’s short-haul fleet.
Being a pilot is the dream, he admits, but the prohibitive training costs – £100,000 or more – put it out of reach. For an enthusiast, he reckons the job is the next best thing. Last year he had to tow the Concorde that still stands at the edge of the airfield across for an exhibition: “It was the first time one had moved in years – incredible to see in the rear-view mirror.”
Chris Thackaberry, network traffic controller, Transport for London
The day starts in Victoria Station House overlooking the bus terminus, a grand old building that looks considerably less so inside, where Chris’s desk is surrounded by hundreds of cardboard diversion signs.
About 500 of the capital’s 19,000 bus stops are on his patch in Westminster – home to some of Britain’s most congested streets, where dozens of bus routes cross. Roadworks are the bane of the bus and Thackaberry’s job is to keep them moving – armed with a van, pliers and zip ties.
Sometimes he can plan for roadworks months ahead. But other days are less predictable, when life suddenly blocks a route: “It could be a broken-down vehicle or a burst water main, but I’ve had windows falling out of buildings, I’ve had a collapsed horse on a bridge. I had an upside down Lamborghini in Piccadilly … I don’t know if it was sticking to the 20mph limit.”
![Man in a red and yellow hi-vis vest inside a van, picking up a red and yellow ‘Buses on diversion’ signs.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/859abfebc10dcb8ea0049f66e031d815e59075b2/625_0_9375_7500/master/9375.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
His incident response van contains an orderly standing desk area and even a printer to rustle up more signs if needed, as well as spill dry sacks, ready to suck up any diesel or oil leaked over the road.
It also has two cylinders affixed to the wall containing “spit kits” – swabs to pick up any saliva aimed at staff, with clear bags to seal, ready to take the evidence to the police. “It’s just part and parcel of when you’re working in London, for anyone in uniform.”
In a sweltering Trafalgar Square, as he hunts in the midst of four lanes of traffic to hitch his cardboard signs to any available piece of spare street furniture, the complexity of the puzzle becomes clearer.
“There’s so many routes go through here, we’re fighting with ourselves for space.”
after newsletter promotion
Sarah, railway signaller, York
Gone are most of the signal boxes of old: these days, Britain’s railway is mostly controlled from one of 12 remote centres. From a windowless room in York, trains right down the East Coast mainline are guided on their way.
“In the old days, it was lever pulling,” says Sarah. “Now it’s a click of the mouse instead. Like a computer game scenario, but it’s real track, real trains, real people. We have to manually click, signal to signal, for every train that comes through our patch.”
Signallers have five screens at eye level showing the railway, and five above with timetables and traffic management information.
“When you first start the job, it feels so far removed. There’s no windows, it’s like a black hole in the middle of the building, but you are signalling trains from York all the way into King’s Cross. I remember thinking: ‘How many hundreds of people are on that train we’re signalling?’”
Anything from a circuit failure to a trespasser to a sick passenger on a train can hold up the lines. “Our job initially in any incident is to make the area safe – that’s first and foremost. And then we look for a workaround, to keep trains moving. The days when there are serious incidents are few and far between. But every day there’s something.”
Jamie *, public service vehicle engineer, Manchester
At Jamie’s bus depot, servicing the Bee Network, the first shift starts at 5am and the last ends at 1am, but engineers might stay through the night with a breakdown.
“In the daytime it’s routine: vehicles are inspected by law on a monthly basis,” he says. “But engineers have bus driving licences too, if a bus was to break down, often we’d take another one out to the driver to keep the service running.”
With city buses that stop and start frequently, there is typically more treatment and maintenance. And newer vehicles don’t necessarily mean less work, he says: “They bring a lot of new issues and we’re constantly learning, going back to college on courses to learn the tech.
“Electric buses haven’t made the job easier – but they and the new diesel engines are clean. Working back in the day, it was a hell of a lot dirtier, especially in depots indoors or undercover,” says the vehicle engineer.
He will check each bus’s brakes, emissions tests and inspect the nuts and bolts everywhere from the underside to the driver’s cab. “We see a lot in the press about the conditions in the cab, but we’re cleaning those buses: it’s like a greenhouse, and the heat from the engines also comes into our workshop.
“Even the drivers don’t understand what engineers do – I always say we are the forgotten people. But without us, no wheel would turn.”
Frankie *, baggage handler, Gatwick
The thing people don’t understand, explains Frankie, is that the placement of bags in the hold is not random. “It’s all done on weight distribution. You have to put baggage where you’re told – it is a very specific job, you do not deviate.”
At many airports, larger aircraft such as long-haul planes are loaded with bags already in large crates, lifted into position by machine. But short-haul flights at Gatwick are loaded manually. “An average bag is about 20kg and the average load is 90 bags off, 90 on, for three or four people. If you do eight turns a day, that’s nearly 30 tonnes your team is lifting. You get fitter – it’s like going to the gym, you end up lifting heavier and heavier bags.”
Passengers who fear for their luggage often make the job harder: “The worst thing is shrink-wrapped bags. It’s slippery, harder to hold on to, and less grip for the belt to pull up. And those straps around bags, they can get jammed in the belts and break them.
“People don’t realise how damaging it can be – and pointless. If you’re on a flight where customs do spot checks, they go for the bags that are wrapped. And there is so much CCTV and security. If I get caught opening a bag, I’d lose my job – why would I risk that?”
There are, says Frankie, more women doing the job now: “It’s getting more female-friendly. A lot of people choose this type of job to get into aviation: they want to be pilots or crew eventually, and just want to be around planes any way they can.”
* Names have been changed
summary: This article highlights the vital, often unseen roles of various workers who keep England's transport systems running smoothly. From airport operations and traffic control to railway signalling, bus engineering, and baggage handling, these professionals manage daily challenges far from the public eye. Despite the difficulties and lack of recognition, their dedication ensures the safety and continuation of public transport.
key_points: Jack Quantick-Thorne manages runway maintenance, aircraft marshalling, airfield monitoring, and bird dispersal at Heathrow Airport.
Chris Thackaberry uses an incident response van and cardboard diversion signs to navigate roadworks and unexpected obstructions for London buses.
Sarah operates multiple screens from a windowless control center in York to manually signal trains along the East Coast mainline.
Jamie and other public service vehicle engineers maintain Manchester's Bee Network buses, performing routine inspections and adapting to new vehicle technologies.
Frankie handles manual baggage loading for short-haul flights at Gatwick, carefully managing weight distribution and lifting significant tonnage daily.

title: Pet owners at risk of being ripped off by private equity firms as vet ownership rules change
author: Helena Horton
content:
Pet owners have been warned that they could be unknowingly ripped off by private equity firms who have bought local vet clinics, after the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) removed requirements for multinational companies to disclose which practices they own.
The CMA recently ran an investigation into the monopolisation of vet practices, and found that the lack of competition and transparency of ownership had led to high prices and a lack of information for customers. Pet owners were often unaware their local vet practice could be owned by an international private equity company.
It revealed pet owners pay 16.6% more on average at large vet groups than at independent practices. It said the £6.3bn market was not fit for purpose and needed to be modernised.
![A veterinary nurse holding a rabbit in a surgery.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b00d50bd00b16aac16e7868b2011dac0f1ced290/0_0_5557_3709/master/5557.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
As a result, the CMA and ministers announced new rules in a white paper earlier this summer proposing capping prescriptions for pet medicine at £21 and more transparency over ownership.
But the Progressive Veterinary Association (PVA), made up of a group of vets, has threatened the government body with a judicial review, after the CMA changed the wording in its plans in a way the PVA says allows multinational companies to obscure their ownership of vet practices.
More than 60% of veterinary practices are owned in whole or in part by six groups: CVS, Pets at Home, Medivet, IVC and VetPartners, which are owned by private equity investors; and Linnaeus, whose parent company is Mars Petcare, a subsidiary of the US confectionery group Mars.
Rather than the name of one of the large multinational companies or private equity investors being listed as the owner of the vet practice, the new rules will allow corporates to use a brand name, or the name of the original independent practice.
The initial wording of the orders from the CMA said that vets had to disclose their ownership and name the “corporate vet group”. This language has been softened to “network or group”, meaning the name of the vet practice or subsidiary of the company could be named, instead of the large conglomerate.
![A dog enjoys being petted by a young boy](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/47211042de9ee2bc3e9bece6989a07ac2bbec0f1/0_0_7151_5003/master/7151.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Dr Iain McGill, a director of the PVA, told the Guardian: “This is bad news for pet-owners and their animals. Ultimately, large corporations would be allowed to hide the fact that they are the ultimate controller of local vet practices and operate behind sometimes misleading brand names.
“Where they have a choice, pet owners often prefer independent practices, which the CMA found, on average, to be cheaper than corporate practices. It would be good to hear from prime minister Andy Burnham that he is on the side of small British-owned businesses rather than often foreign private equity and corporate investors.”
The CMA told vets who complained that the disclosure of the ultimate parent company names might not be of any meaningful benefit to pet owners. They added that these names can be unrecognisable corporate names and that pet owners are more familiar with the high street vet or pet company names.
But the vets argued that pet owners have the right to know if their local vet was owned by a large conglomerate.
The PVA said in its submission to the government regulator: “The suggestion that accurate corporate ownership information may provide no meaningful benefit to pet owners perhaps rather underestimates the intelligence of the average pet owner. Knowing full ownership information is necessary so that pet owners can make an informed choice. Lack of informed market choices is likely to lead to less competition and pet owner detriment.”
A CMA spokesperson said: “It is critical that pet owners know whether their local practice is part of a national group or locally owned, and we are confident the changes we are making will achieve this. In future, all practices will have to make ownership links clear by using brand names that people recognise on signs and online. We will no longer have the unacceptable situation of people thinking they are using a local practice when in fact it is part of a bigger group.
“We consulted extensively on this. Our proposals were supported by large and small vet practices and consumer groups, and we made our decision on this in our final report in March. We’re now considering comments on exactly how the changes should be put in place, to make sure they are clear and workable for pet owners and vets.”
summary: Pet owners face warnings that private equity firms and multinational companies are quietly taking over local veterinary clinics, leading to higher prices and a lack of transparency. An investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) found that large vet groups charge on average 16.6% more than independent practices. Although new rules were proposed to increase transparency, the CMA adjusted the wording to allow corporations to use brand names rather than the ultimate parent company's name, prompting criticism and a threatened judicial review from the Progressive Veterinary Association.
key_points: Pet owners pay an average of 16.6% more at large vet groups compared to independent practices.
More than 60% of veterinary practices are owned by six major corporate or private equity-backed groups.
The CMA altered its rules to allow practices to display brand names rather than disclosing ultimate parent company names.
The Progressive Veterinary Association threatened a judicial review, arguing the change allows corporations to hide their true ownership.
The CMA defended the policy, stating that familiar brand names and online notices will provide clearer ownership links than unrecognisable corporate names.

title: The US got Meta to change Instagram and Facebook. Europe wants in.
author: Eliza Gkritsi
content:
BRUSSELS — The United States just made Meta change how it treats kids. The pressure's now on for Europe to prove its tougher tech laws can do the same — or go even further.
Forty-seven U.S. states settled a landmark lawsuit with Meta for $18 billion on Wednesday, agreeing with the tech giant to set guardrails on its addictive design to better protect teenagers from harm. It is the culmination of a yearslong battle in one of the largest consumer protection settlements in U.S. history.
From Brussels’ vantage point, it’s both a win for online safety and a loss of face for the European regulator, which has tried to get the social media giant to change its ways for years.
summary: Forty-seven U.S. states have settled an $18 billion landmark lawsuit with Meta, establishing guardrails on addictive platform designs to protect teenagers. This major consumer protection settlement puts pressure on European regulators, who have spent years attempting to achieve similar changes in social media safety. The event is viewed from Brussels as both a victory for online safety and a loss of face for European authorities.
key_points: Forty-seven U.S. states settled an $18 billion lawsuit with Meta regarding teen safety.
The settlement establishes new guardrails on Meta's addictive product designs.
The agreement increases pressure on European regulators to enforce tougher tech laws.
Brussels views the U.S. settlement as both an online safety win and a regulatory loss of face.

title: Healey eyes windfall tax on banks and oil companies
author: Camilla Turner; Tony Diver
content:
![John Healey wants his Budget to be seen as a 'low-key affair'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000496043846_17880288004210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_4lZL6XGyKd1IzVfh-3zqv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![John Healey wants his Budget to be seen as a 'low-key affair'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000496043846_17880288004210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_4lZL6XGyKd1IzVfh-3zqv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
John Healey is considering a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in his first Budget, The Telegraph understands.
Treasury officials are discussing both policies as they try to find ways to plug a £4.7bn hole in the public finances while seeking to avoid direct tax increases on individuals.
The Chancellor is understood to want next month’s Budget to be framed as low-key and to make sure that inevitable tax rises are much lower than those pushed through by Rachel Reeves, his predecessor.
Hitting companies while shielding individual taxpayers would allow Mr Healey to regain fiscal headroom damaged by high gilt rates and the impact of the war in Iran, while also raising a few billion pounds to spend on defence and other priorities.
Increasing taxes on banks, which have enjoyed substantial profits, was described by one official as “low-hanging fruit” that Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, and his Chancellor would find hard to ignore, according to Bloomberg.
Treasury officials monitoring the economic fallout from the US-Iran war have noted that BP’s profits more than doubled between April and June because of elevated oil prices, leading some officials to propose increased taxes on the windfall for fossil fuel companies.
![A woman uses her phone to record as smoke and flames rise at the site of airstrikes on an oil depot in Tehran](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/03/10/TELEMMGLPICT000470855930_17731577013000_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq1cd_6dGp6tKmReQCWjBtJRNzhCo6wqq6_olW02V7_aM.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
One option under consideration would be for the Treasury to launch a time-limited “windfall” tax on banking profits, modelled on a similar policy applied to oil and gas giants since the start of the war in Ukraine. Mr Healey could also extend the windfall tax on the oil and gas sector beyond March 2030, and increase the levy.
The discussions over taxation come after Mr Burnham’s plan to force the embattled Thames Water into administration as a “week one” priority was shelved following an intervention by Treasury officials.
![The 'low-hanging fruit' of a windfall tax on banks would be difficult for Andy Burnham to pass up, financial experts said](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/politics/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499433451_17880289666060_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqAJ7EFHYU_DkfdKivFZF_lfDyNODtUQ2nBmcr3kRMXzg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A source close to discussions told The Telegraph that, following some frank discussions with the Treasury, Downing Street backed down on plans to intervene to save the debt-laden water company.
“The Treasury position has never wavered – that there is less money to play with than we would like and we have to be really careful about spending taxpayers’ money,” the source said.
“There is an inter-Whitehall war going on between those who have to make the sums add up and the rhetoric.”
The source explained that the water industry “needs a huge amount of investment and it is operationally very stressed”, adding that the Treasury “knows that it is not a good use of taxpayer money. It is a very risky investment. The Treasury is holding firm”.
Treasury sources said they would not characterise the discussions over Thames Water as a “war” with Downing Street, suggesting instead that the discussions were a sign of a “well-functioning government”.
Mr Burnham’s belief that utilities should be under stronger public control had “not changed”, a government spokesman said.
“This Government is looking at how we can give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible,” they added. “We’re bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment.”
UK Finance, the financial industry’s trade association, has urged Mr Healey not to launch any further taxes on banks or risk driving away investment from the City of London.
In a letter to the Chancellor, the sector warned against a “damaging” raid on the industry.
Treasury officials told The Telegraph that the Government kept bank taxes “under review”, to ensure the “objectives of growth and responsible fiscal policy are appropriately balanced”.
British banks already pay one of the highest tax rates in the world at nearly 47 per cent, according to UK Finance.
They pointed out that banking “accounts for over £1 in every £25 of economic output”, and that the UK tax environment played a “meaningful role in decisions about where individual banks invest, deploy capital and allocate jobs”.
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has also warned Mr Healey that raising taxes on UK banks could trigger staff to move abroad. Sir Howard Davies, the former chairman of NatWest, has also cautioned Mr Burnham against the move, saying it risked sending banking activities abroad.
The top four UK banks have dramatically outperformed the rest of the economy in the past year, posting an average 21 per cent increase in profits in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025.
Since its introduction in May 2022, the oil and gas levy – officially called the energy profits levy – has raised £9.1bn.
Robin Allan, chairman of the Association of British Independent Exploration Companies, told The Telegraph that extending or increasing the levy on oil and gas companies “would be acts of economic madness”.
He added that it would “further damage the fragile economy of our domestic oil and gas industry” and said his group would write to the Treasury and seek a meeting with ministers to discuss it.
The Chancellor is also believed to be considering ways to borrow more to finance infrastructure in a manner that he could claim was compatible with the fiscal rules.
Sources close to Mr Healey said the Budget would focus on his priorities of fiscal stability and breathing space for people and businesses. Treasury sources have said the Budget will be a low-key affair, with several major policy decisions, such as welfare reform, postponed until next year.
They said they would not comment on speculation around tax policy ahead of the Budget.
A Treasury spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on his priorities, which will boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode.
“As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on proposals made.”
summary: Chancellor John Healey is considering a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in his upcoming Budget to help plug a £4.7 billion shortfall in public finances while shielding individual taxpayers from direct increases. Treasury officials are discussing a time-limited banking tax and potentially extending or increasing the existing energy profits levy on fossil fuel companies. The proposed measures have drawn warnings from industry groups and financial leaders who caution that higher levies could drive investment and jobs out of the UK.
key_points: Treasury officials are exploring a windfall tax on banks and fossil fuel companies to plug a £4.7bn budget gap without raising direct taxes on individuals.
Options under consideration include a time-limited tax on banking profits and extending or increasing the existing energy profits levy on oil and gas giants beyond March 2030.
Industry representatives and banking executives, including JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon, have warned that increasing bank taxes could drive investment and staff abroad.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's initial plan to force Thames Water into administration was shelved following resistance from Treasury officials concerned about taxpayer risk.
The upcoming Budget is intended to be low-key, with major policy decisions such as welfare reform postponed until the following year.

title: How can plug-in solar kits be 1,260W when the limit is 800W?
author: Jeff Meyer
content:
Plug-in solar panels are now legal in Great Britain, but anyone browsing the first systems to go on sale may have spotted what, on the surface, looks like a contradiction with the government’s new rules for compliance.
The new rules limit plug-in solar to 800W, yet Argos is already selling UKSOL kits labelled 890W, 1,030W and even 1,260W. So how can they be allowed under the new rules?
The answer is that those larger numbers describe the combined generating capacity of the solar panels, while the legal limit applies to the amount of power the system can feed into your home.
Under the government’s new plug-in solar specification, a compliant system can have a maximum apparent AC power output of 800VA – generally presented to consumers as an 800W limit. The plug-in panels have a microinverter built into the system that ensures it can’t supply more than this amount to your household circuit.
Read more: First look at plug-in solar panels
Get a free quote for solar panels for your home
Panels and inverters have different ratings
Solar panels generate direct current (DC) electricity, which passes through the system’s microinverter and is converted into alternating current (AC) electricity, which is used by the appliances in your home.
The plug-in solar panels and the inverter therefore have their own separate power ratings.
Take, for example, the £989 UKSOL Pro Max kit currently listed by Argos. It includes two 630W solar panels, giving it a total nominal panel capacity of 1,260W, but those panels feed into an 800W microinverter. No matter how much electricity the panels are capable of producing, the inverter still limits the AC output supplied to the house.
That means a system can legitimately contain more than 800W of solar panel capacity without exceeding the plug-in solar limit.
Read more: Plug-in vs installed solar panels
Why install 1,260W of panels if you can only use 800W?
Your next question is probably: What’s the point, then, of getting panels with more than 800W capacity? It’s a good question. It might sound wasteful, but solar panels rarely produce their headline output on a continuous basis.
A panel’s wattage is measured under standard laboratory test conditions. But in the real world, output varies according to factors such as the time of day, season, cloud cover, temperature, shading and the direction and angle of the panels.
Using a system that’s more than 800W of panel capacity can therefore help an 800W microinverter get closer to its maximum output for more of the day.
Argos, for example, says the oversized 1,260W panel capacity in its UKSOL kit is intended to maximise generation during poorer weather. On a cloudy morning, the panels might collectively produce considerably less than their theoretical maximum, meaning all of that electricity can still pass through the inverter.
When conditions are good enough for the panels to generate more power than the inverter can handle, the inverter simply caps its AC output at its maximum. This is sometimes known as “clipping”.
Read more: Are plug-in solar panels worth buying?
What does the 800W limit actually mean?
The important figure for shoppers is therefore not necessarily the number printed on the solar panels.
Britain’s new rules allow a compliant plug-in solar product with a maximum apparent power output of 800VA. The government specification defines a plug-in solar product as a complete system including at least one solar panel, a grid-following microinverter, a manufacturer-supplied lead and UK plug, and a mounting system.
So seeing a 1,030W or 1,260W plug-in solar kit doesn’t mean a manufacturer or retailer has found a loophole in the new 800W rules. It simply means the panels have been oversized relative to the inverter. What reaches your household electrical circuit is still capped at 800W.
summary: While Great Britain limits plug-in solar systems to an 800W power output feed into a home, retailers like Argos sell kits with panel capacities exceeding 1,000W. This is permissible because the legal limit applies strictly to the AC output regulated by the system's built-in microinverter rather than the combined solar panel capacity. Oversizing the panels helps maximize power generation during less-than-ideal weather conditions like cloudy mornings.
key_points: British regulations restrict plug-in solar systems to a maximum apparent AC power output of 800VA, commonly referred to as an 800W limit.
Higher numbers on solar kits (such as 1,260W) represent the combined generation capacity of the panels, not the output sent to the home.
A built-in microinverter caps the electricity supplied to the household circuit at the legal 800W limit, a process known as clipping.
Oversizing the solar panel capacity allows the system to reach the maximum 800W output more frequently during suboptimal conditions like cloudy weather.
