The project is expected to create over 3,000 direct jobs and more than 8,100 indirect jobs in the region.
key_points: SpaceX plans to build a $100bn launch site called Starbase, Louisiana, spanning 125,000 acres.
Construction is scheduled to start next year, with the first Starship flight targeted for 2029.
The project will add more than 3,000 direct jobs with high average wages, plus over 8,100 indirect jobs.
The facility is designed to support thousands of Starship flights a year to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

title: Labour’s reforms on zero-hours contracts are terrible for young workers
author: Helen Dickinson; Allen Simpson; Shevaun Haviland
content:
![People walk into the the Job Centre Plus in Staines, Surrey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/25/TELEMMGLPICT000402990610_17876741681370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhxIBykwsigX1ySZvqBRpDtHhMh81Y8GqX3ipA8YMo0k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![People walk into the the Job Centre Plus in Staines, Surrey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/25/TELEMMGLPICT000402990610_17876741681370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhxIBykwsigX1ySZvqBRpDtHhMh81Y8GqX3ipA8YMo0k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Government’s consultation on reforms to zero-hours contracts and shifts has closed. What government decides to do will be critical for millions of workers and the businesses employing them.
At its heart, the reforms mean workers on zero-hours or low-hours contracts who frequently work more than their contracted hours must be offered a guaranteed number of hours based on their working pattern. Employers also face new rules around how they offer shifts and compensate workers if those shifts are cancelled, moved, or cut short at limited notice.
These reforms offer a once-in-a-generation opportunity to stamp out bad practices and target unscrupulous employers – an ambition everyone firmly supports. But if government gets the implementation wrong, measures designed to give people greater security at work will have the opposite effect: fewer jobs, fewer hours and fewer routes into work, particularly for young people.
Our organisations represent businesses employing millions of people and driving local growth in every postcode. Their message is clear: the rising cost and complexity of employment is already making them think twice about hiring.
The latest ONS figures show a jobs market at breaking point. Unemployment at 4.9 per cent, vacancies at a five-year low, and private-sector pay growth at its weakest since 2020. More than one million young people are not in education, employment or training, while the war in Iran is adding to the squeeze on household finances.
Businesses are absorbing billions in additional employment costs. In the last two years, retailers have shouldered roughly £6.5bn, while hospitality has faced more than £4bn, with both sectors combined losing around 155,000 jobs since the 2024 Budget.
The Government’s own analysis estimates its reforms could cost employers up to £2.9bn a year, before wider costs of Employment Rights Act measures, including changes to statutory sick pay, are even taken into account.
Businesses need the flexibility to offer their workforce extra hours to cope with busy periods. A pub, hotel or high street store is significantly busier because of seasonal peaks, good weather, tourism or a major sporting event. But if this forces them to make a permanent commitment to those extra hours, then fewer additional shifts will be offered, or will be offered only to those already above the “low hours” threshold.
Just look at the World Cup. The Government, rightly, extended licensing hours mere days before England played Mexico, meaning thousands of pubs had to staff up at late notice for one of the biggest games of the tournament. Willing hospitality teams took advantage to earn some more money. Flexibility was good for our teams, our customers, and the economy.
Under these reforms, which require a yet-to-be-defined “reasonable notice” of shifts, will that be possible in the future?
If these reforms force businesses to make a permanent commitment to those extra hours and restrict the flexibility of our sectors, then fewer additional shifts will be offered, or will be offered only to those already above the “low hours” threshold. Reforms intended to create greater security for those on low hours could end up hurting the very people they aim to support.
This matters. Flexibility is not the same as exploitation. Flexible work provides millions of people – including students, parents, carers and those looking for their first job – a way to fit work around their busy lives.
There is a better way to target bad practice. Guaranteed Hours legislation is meant to eliminate exploitative zero-hours contracts. Setting the threshold at eight hours a week or fewer will ensure it is focused on the people who need it. Similarly, the period used to establish someone’s regular working pattern should be 52 weeks, ensuring temporary seasonal increases in hiring are not mistaken for permanent ones.
Businesses also need time to prepare. With employers already adapting to wider changes under the Employment Rights Act, there should be the maximum implementation time given the complexity of these reforms. The Government should use that time to work with businesses and unions to get the details right.
None of this means weakening protections for workers. Unscrupulous employers should be targeted and bad practice stamped out. But Britain cannot afford to turn reforms intended to improve job security into another barrier to getting a job. Not when millions of people are already struggling to find work.
Ministers now have a chance to get this right. Target the bad employers, protect workers, but do not make good employers think twice about hiring. With Britain facing a jobs crisis, we cannot afford reforms that close the very doors into work we most need open.
Helen Dickinson is Chief Executive of the BRC. Allen Simpson is the Chief Executive of
UK Hospitality. And Shevaun Haviland is Director General at the British Chambers of Commerce
summary: The government's proposed reforms to zero-hours contracts aim to provide greater security by requiring guaranteed hours and compensation for short-notice shift changes. However, business leaders warn that the rising costs and restricted flexibility could lead to fewer jobs and hours, particularly harming young workers and struggling sectors. They suggest setting a clear low-hours threshold, using a 52-week reference period, and allowing maximum implementation time to avoid creating barriers to employment.
key_points: Reforms require employers to offer guaranteed hours based on regular patterns and follow new rules for shift cancellations and changes.
Business groups warn the rules could cost employers up to £2.9bn a year and reduce vital flexibility needed for seasonal peaks and events.
The current jobs market faces challenges including 4.9 percent unemployment, five-year low vacancies, and over one million young people not in education, employment, or training.
Authors recommend setting the guaranteed hours threshold at eight hours or fewer and using a 52-week period to prevent temporary seasonal increases from becoming permanent obligations.

title: Burnham announces plan for 10,000 work experience placements for young people – UK politics live
author: Taz Ali; Julia Kollewe
content:
Burnham calls on businesses to offer work experience opportunities for young people
PA has reported some remarks by the prime minister on his visit to Sainsbury’s this morning, where he is announcing his work experience plan.
Andy Burnham said the UK needs more employers to step up and offer work experience opportunities for young people.
“This is a really positive development today,” he said.
He continued:
One of the biggest British brands out there, Sainsbury’s, coming forward and saying 10,000 placements for young people, work placements, apprenticeships. This is exactly what we need.
We need a national drive to challenge youth unemployment and give more opportunities for our young people, and I would ask other businesses to do the same.
We have a huge challenge – too many young people are out of work – but it can be fixed.
I think we need to fix the education system, which is what I’m doing as well, giving young people technical paths alongside the academic route.
But then we need employers to step forward and offer those work placements too.”
PA followed the prime minister around as he spoke to 14 to 16-year-olds on a summer careers programme and shoppers at Sainsbury’s in Nine Elms, south-west London.
One man at the self-checkouts told him he hailed from Manchester and “London isn’t for me”. Andy Burnham replied: “I’m adapting.”
Burnham told the teenagers about his first work experience, when his interest in languages meant he was placed at a travel agent in St Helens.
“The experience was, let’s say, hard,” he said, adding “it wasn’t wasted” as he realised that line of work was not for him.
“You won’t fall on your feet straight away,” he told the young people, noting “it takes a little while” to find the right career path.
Prime minister Andy Burnham speaks to members of staff and young people during his visit to Sainsbury's in Nine Elms, London. Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PA
Burnham was joined by London mayor Sadiq Khan and work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden, after the government and supermarket chain announced a programme to help more young people in deprived areas into work
The prime minister has called on more businesses to offer work experience opportunities for young people to tackle youth unemployment. He said the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is a “huge challenge” which employers need to help address.
Andy Burnham accompanied by mayor of London Sadiq Khan and work and pensions Secretary Pat McFadden during his visit to Sainsbury's . Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PA
“I was a huge fan of what Dolly did around literacy around the world. I was culture secretary when her libraries were first coming through and the books that went into communities across Britain, you know, what a legacy to leave.
And it was so moving to hear about her dad and how that experience made her want to give back so much. So, yeah, she leaves that legacy as well as obviously great music that people will treasure for ever.”
Government to look at ways to bring energy bills down after price cap increase, says Burnham
Answering questions on the energy price cap, which will increase by 4% from October to a three-year high, Burnham said he acknowledged how “difficult” it will be for people to deal with rising energy bills, but that the government will look at ways to bring them down.
He told reporters:
It’s why, within days of taking office, I announced that we would remove VAT off electricity bills to give people that little bit of help.
That kicks in from October.
We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.
And we’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”
When asked by reporters whether Britons should be worried about possible Russian attacks on the UK, Burnham responded: “It’s a challenging situation when we look around the world right now.
“But from what we’re doing, people need to be sure of this: We’re doing what we’ve done since the start of this conflict, which is to provide that back up support to Ukraine to be able to defend themselves, because they do need to do that.”
He added: “I visited Ukraine to send a really clear message to the Ukrainian people that Britain isn’t changing course. We said we would support them. We are supporting them and that won’t change.”
Prime minister Andy Burnham and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday. Photograph: Ukrainian Presidency/SIPA/Shutterstock
Burnham calls on businesses to offer work experience opportunities for young people
PA has reported some remarks by the prime minister on his visit to Sainsbury’s this morning, where he is announcing his work experience plan.
Andy Burnham said the UK needs more employers to step up and offer work experience opportunities for young people.
“This is a really positive development today,” he said.
He continued:
One of the biggest British brands out there, Sainsbury’s, coming forward and saying 10,000 placements for young people, work placements, apprenticeships. This is exactly what we need.
We need a national drive to challenge youth unemployment and give more opportunities for our young people, and I would ask other businesses to do the same.
We have a huge challenge – too many young people are out of work – but it can be fixed.
I think we need to fix the education system, which is what I’m doing as well, giving young people technical paths alongside the academic route.
But then we need employers to step forward and offer those work placements too.”
While we wait to hear from Andy Burnham, here is a report by my colleague Richard Partington from earlier this monthon the Neet crisis, an issue that has risen up the government’s agenda:
Government looking at 'fundamental reforms' to lower energy bills
Julia Kollewe
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy sectary, said the government will explore “what more we can do” to help those struggling with high bills, via “fundamental reforms” including investment in renewable energy.
Families will be understandably concerned about the cost of energy bills this winter, which is being driven up by the Iran war.
Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.
This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.
The government is looking at “fundamental reforms” to drive down energy bills for good, the energy secretary said.
Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh arrives at 10 Downing Street for prime minister Andy Burnham’s first cabinet meeting on 21 July. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Speaking to Sky News, Fahnbulleh said:
If you look at energy bills, if you look at how much of a family’s finances it is taking up, it is far too expensive.
So, whether that is short-term support that we’re providing to provide a bit of breathing space, which is what the government has done and will continue looking at that, or more fundamental reforms that we need to make to the energy market to drive down bills for good, we are absolutely determined to do that.
She argued renewable energy investment is “absolutely critical” to breaking the link between high gas costs and bills.
Fahbulleh also said she was “frustrated” global events had increased bills in the UK but would not be drawn on criticising Donald Trump for starting the war in Iran.
For the latest updates, follow our business live blog here:
Opening summary: Burnham to announce plan for 10,000 work experience placements for young people
Morning, and welcome to our UK politics blog. Prime minister Andy Burnham is nipping to the shops this morning to announce a plan to get teenagers working, as the government seeks to tackle the “youth unemployment crisis”.
Burnham will be in Sainsbury’s to welcome the supermarket’s plan to offer 10,000 work experience placements in deprived areas, focusing on communities with a high number of young people not in education, employment or training, otherwise called Neets.
Here are the deets: from October, Sainsbury’s will offer work experience and skills sessions for young people from the age of 14 in England, Wales and Scotland. Running for a year, it is hoped the plan will “help young people build confidence, gain experience and get a foot in the door,” Burnham said.
Prime minister Andy Burnham at No10 North in Manchester . Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian
“I encourage more businesses across the country to do the same,” he added. “Access to opportunity and work experience shouldn’t depend on who you know, it should be within reach for every young person wherever they live – and that’s what I’m determined to deliver.”
The prime minister is due to speak to the media from about 9am, but other headlines this morning may overshadow the press briefing.
Ofgem, the energy regulator for Great Britain, announced the energy price cap will increase by 4% from October, meaning millions of households will face the highest energy charges in three years this winter. The Guardian’s energy correspondent Jillian Ambrosereported the following:
Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap, months after climbing 13% at the start of July to take account of soaring global energy market prices caused by the war on Iran.
Ofgem, said the new rate for about 22m households was equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical household’s gas and electricity use, compared with the rise to £1,663 for the July to September period.
As the bill rises in consecutive quarters the typical household will pay an extra £350 a year more than in 2024, when the Labour government came to power with a promise that it would cut bills by £300 a year by the end of the decade.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited a Sainsbury's in London to announce a plan aimed at tackling youth unemployment by encouraging businesses to offer work experience. During the visit, Sainsbury's committed to providing 10,000 work placements and apprenticeships for young people in deprived areas. Additionally, officials addressed rising energy bills following a 4% increase in the energy price cap set for October, noting that the government is looking at short-term relief and long-term reforms.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a work experience plan to tackle youth unemployment and help young people not in education, employment, or training (Neet).
Supermarket chain Sainsbury's agreed to provide 10,000 work placements and apprenticeships for young people starting in October.
The energy price cap is set to increase by 4% in October, reaching a three-year high.
The government stated it will look into ways to bring energy bills down in the long term, including removing VAT on electricity and exploring renewable energy investments.

title: FTSE 100 Live: Shell and BP drag on blue-chips as oil slides
author: Felix Armstrong; Samuel Norman
content:
![BP gas station sign displaying fuel prices: Regular Unleaded 184.9 and Regular Diesel 205.9.](https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/01KP8F9QA8Q6X6PKSXMMTQSDWF-1-e1787730663539.jpg?w=742) 
Welcome back to the City AM FTSE 100 liveblog.
The UK’s blue-chip index has slipped on Wednesday morning, dragged down by oil majors BP and Shell in response to a continued slide in oil prices.
Brent crude – the international benchmark – fell by more than two per cent on Wednesday to $86 per barrel, extending this week’s losses. On Tuesday night, Pakistan’s army chief said significant progress was being made towards a US-Iran peace deal.
Reports that Iran and Oman are nearing a deal to secure an “interim” reopening of the Strait of Hormuz are a further sign that oil price pressures could begin to ease.
Dan Coatsworth, AJ Bell’s head of markets, said: “Despite the pressure lower oil prices put on the shares of index heavyweights BP and Shell, the FTSE 100 managed to make some progress [on Tuesday]. It was supported by gains in the retail, aviation and housebuilding sectors.
“These areas have typically been beneficiaries when hopes of a resolution to the Iran conflict emerge, given the implications for inflation and borrowing costs if shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz are unblocked.”
This morning, energy regulator Ofgem hiked its cap on household bills by four per cent to an annual bill of £1,723, putting fresh pressure on Andy Burnham’s cost-of-living agenda.
The new price cap, which will cover the three months from October, comes as the Iran war and its global impact on energy prices rumbles on. Economists said last quarter’s price cap rise contributed to higher UK inflation.
Across the Atlantic, the emerging trade war between the US and Canada was taken up a notch overnight. Canada’s finance minister unveiled a $20bn package of retaliatory tariffs against its neighbour after President Trump stepped up his rhetorical attacks on his northern neighbour.
We’ll be bringing you the latest market updates and analysis.
summary: The UK's FTSE 100 slipped on Wednesday morning as oil majors BP and Shell declined alongside a drop in Brent crude prices to $86 per barrel. Hopes of easing oil price pressures stem from reports of progress on a US-Iran peace deal and a potential interim reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Ofgem raised its household energy price cap by four per cent to £1,723 starting in October, and Canada announced a $20bn package of retaliatory tariffs against the US.
key_points: Brent crude fell by more than two per cent to $86 per barrel, dragging down oil majors BP and Shell on the FTSE 100.
Reports indicate progress on a US-Iran peace deal and a potential interim reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Ofgem increased its household energy price cap by four per cent to an annual bill of £1,723 beginning in October.
Canada's finance minister unveiled a $20bn package of retaliatory tariffs against the US amid escalating trade tensions.

title: Heatwaves show UK must do more to promote cycling and walking, campaigners say
author: Damien Gayle
content:
Dozens of civil society groups have demanded the UK government do more to promote cycling and walking, after this summer’s extreme heat exposed the desperate need to decarbonise transport.
This summer’s heatwaves and wildfires were “immediate, real-world manifestations of the climate emergency”, the groups said, making reform of transport – responsible for more carbon emissions than any other sector in the UK – an urgent priority.
Last year, domestic transport was responsible for almost a third of the UK’s net greenhouse gas emissions – with the total emissions from the sector increasing 2% over the previous year.
The groups call for a “modal shift” in transport provision. “What that means is creating the conditions which allow people to travel for a higher proportion of the trip by walking, cycling, public transport and shared mobility than by private cars,” said Ben Plowden, the chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport.
The demand comes after Labour appeared to have shelved targets for an increase in trips made by public transport and a reduction in trips using private vehicles.
Before the 2024 election, Labour had committed to setting goals for shifting travel habits away from private vehicles and towards public transport and active travel, such as cycling and walking.
But by this summer the government’s cycling and walking strategy had no broader targets to increase the percentage of total trips made by public transport or to reduce the percentage of total trips made by cars.
The intervention, signed by 54 civil society organisations, was led by the Campaign for Better Transport. Plowden said their call had been lent increased urgency by the summer’s repeated heatwaves and the oil price inflation caused by the US war on Iran.
“That such a range of organisations have come together to make this statement shows the urgent need for stronger action in response to the climate emergency, which has had such a devastating impact on communities across the country this summer,” Plowden said.
“The heatwaves and wildfires, the harm to people, nature and infrastructure, are just a taste of things to come if we do not act urgently.”
The statement called on the government to develop policies including “increasing the proportion of journeys made by public transport, shared transport, walking, wheeling and cycling”, as well as targets to increase the amount of freight carried by trains.
“With the majority of journeys under five miles, this will benefit local communities, making it easier for people to get to shops, schools, health services and see friends and family,” it said.
Plowden said: “It’s really a question around getting on with the sort of investment primarily in local transport improvements that would allow all of those things to happen simultaneously and as part of the same process.
“And we think that that needs to be driven by central government setting an overall target for enabling people to change how they travel, away from private vehicle use and to be able to choose public transport, walks, cycle, wheeled and shared mobility. And of course obviously increase the uptake of electric vehicles as well.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We’re giving people real choice in how they travel by making buses, trains and active travel cheaper, more reliable and easier to access – including lowering the bus fare cap to £2, freezing rail fares, and investing £4.5bn in cycling and walking.
“Rather than restricting how people get around, we’re focused on giving them better alternatives. More broadly, we’re accelerating the UK’s transition to cleaner transport through our ZEV [zero-emission vehicle] mandate, backed by £7.5bn.”
summary: Dozens of civil society groups have urged the UK government to accelerate transport decarbonisation and promote active travel following this summer's extreme heatwaves and wildfires. The coalition, led by the Campaign for Better Transport, demands a shift away from private cars toward walking, cycling, and public transport. This intervention follows concerns that Labour has shelved previous targets to reduce private vehicle trips and increase public transport use. In response, a Department for Transport spokesperson highlighted ongoing investments in cheaper public transport, active travel, and cleaner vehicle mandates.
key_points: Fifty-four civil society organisations demanded the UK government do more to promote walking and cycling.
Domestic transport accounts for nearly a third of the UK's net greenhouse gas emissions.
Campaigners are calling for a modal shift to reduce reliance on private cars.
The Department for Transport stated it is giving people alternatives by investing in cheaper public transport and active travel.

title: ‘Temu Range Rovers’ are taking over Britain
author: Christopher Jasper
content:
Overtaken by a Range Rover in a hurry or startled by a Land Rover the size of a small tank? Take another look, because that luxury 4x4 may in fact be nothing of the sort.
A fleet of Chinese invaders has started to flood Britain’s roads over the last 18 months, and their numbers are far larger than most people imagine.
Copycat Chinese designs of popular models from Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) have become so convincing that, to the uninitiated, there is little to differentiate the bona fide icons from the imported lookalikes costing half the price.
Dubbed “Temu Range Rovers” for their bargain-basement prices, the Asian influx has opened up a new world of motoring possibilities for drivers who put space and comfort ahead of brand. And there are plenty of people taking up the offer.
Jaecoo, which is owned by Chinese automotive giant Chery, has spearheaded the insurgency in Britain.
Its £30,000 Jaecoo 7, a copycat of the Range Rover’s pricier Velar and Evoque models, leapt to the top of the sales charts in March with more than 10,000 purchases – a figure that outperformed its nearest rival by 70pc.
The model, launched in January last year, has been in the UK top 10 for 12 months, but to see it crowned as Britain’s best-selling car came as a shock to the motoring world.
summary: A fleet of affordable Chinese-made copycat vehicles resembling luxury models like Range Rovers has flooded British roads over the past 18 months. Spearheaded by Chery's Jaecoo brand, these lower-priced alternatives offer space and comfort at half the cost of traditional icons. The £30,000 Jaecoo 7 recently became Britain's best-selling car, outperforming its nearest rival by 70 percent.
key_points: Chinese copycat designs of Jaguar Land Rover models have flooded the British car market over the last 18 months.
These vehicles are often dubbed "Temu Range Rovers" due to their bargain-basement prices and resemblance to luxury SUVs.
The Jaecoo 7, owned by Chinese automotive giant Chery, is priced at around £30,000.
The Jaecoo 7 topped the UK sales charts in March with over 10,000 purchases, outperforming its nearest rival by 70 percent.

title: Britons face highest price cap in three years as energy bills rise 4% from October
author: Jillian Ambrose
content:
Millions of households in Great Britain will face the highest energy charges in three years this winter after months of soaring market prices caused the government’s price cap to rise for a second time in three months.
Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October under the new cap, months after climbing 13% at the start of July to take account of soaring global energy market prices caused by the war on Iran.
The energy regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, said the new rate for about 22 million households was equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical household’s gas and electricity use, compared with the rise to £1,663 for the July to September period.
Clare Moriarty, the chief executive of Citizens Advice, said: “It’s another sign of the relentless erosion of living standards across the country: energy bills are simply too high, prices leapfrog incomes, and debt levels continue to grow.”
As the bill rises in consecutive quarters the typical household will pay an extra £350 a year more than in 2024, when the Labour government came to power with a promise that it would cut bills by £300 a year by the end of the decade.
About a third of households that buy their energy via fixed rate deals will not be affected by the change in the energy cap.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said bills were being driven up by the Iran war and the government would “keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills”.
She added: “Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.
“This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year.”
The energy cost increase has reignited calls for the government to help vulnerable households. There have been repeated calls for the government to fund extra measures by raising the windfall taxes on profits made by energy companies and introduce a windfall tax on banks.
“It’s plain common sense,” said Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary. “Banks are raking it in while many up and down the country are struggling to get by – they can well afford to pay more tax to ease the pressure on working people.”
The regulator calculated the average of £1,723 based on the estimated energy use of a typical household. Since July it has assumed lower annual energy use than in previous years because the high cost of energy has forced many households to use less gas and electricity. Under the previous calculations the price cap would have climbed to £1,940.69 from October.
From October, the unit rate for electricity will rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.32p, while gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.97p. However, the actual household bill will depend on how much each consumes.
after newsletter promotion
Energy standing charges, which are charged daily whether you use energy or not, will rise, too. The gas standing charge will climb from 29.04p a day to 29.68p a day, while the daily standing charge for electricity will rise from 57.19p to 54.83p. The combined rate for all these charges is the highest since .
More than a third of households have begun turning down the temperature on their washing machine and radiators in empty rooms since 2023, according to research commissioned by the End Fuel Poverty Coalition.
Meanwhile, when the weather is colder about a fifth of households have begun going to bed early to keep warm or heating only one room to save energy, the survey found.
Simon Francis, the coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: “Some reduction of energy use could be a good thing, caused by better energy efficiency in people’s homes. But sadly, for many households, reductions in energy use have happened simply because people cannot afford to use as much energy as in the past.
“That means that some are demonstrating dangerous behaviours such as cutting back on washing and, for one in 10 members of the public, skipping hot meals to save on energy.”
summary: Millions of households in Great Britain will experience a 4% increase in their energy bills starting in October, raising the typical annual bill to £1,723. The energy regulator Ofgem attributes the rise to soaring global market prices driven by the war on Iran. In response to the mounting cost-of-living pressures, the government has cut VAT on electricity bills and removed other costs, while critics and charities continue to call for additional support and increased windfall taxes.
key_points: Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from October, bringing the typical household bill to £1,723 a year.
The price cap increase affects about 22 million households, though roughly a third on fixed-rate deals are exempt.
The energy secretary stated that the rise is driven by the war on Iran and announced a cut to VAT on electricity bills to limit the increase.
High energy costs have forced many households to reduce consumption, with some cutting back on washing temperatures or skipping hot meals.
Union leaders and charities have renewed calls for the government to fund extra support measures by raising windfall taxes on energy companies and banks.

title: Billionaire investor says he used AI to write critique of former mentee Scott Bessent
author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
content:
Stanley Druckenmiller, a billionaire investor, said he used artificial intelligence to pen his viral Wall Street Journal op-ed in which he sharply criticized the interference of Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, in the US bond market.
Many news outlets, including the Guardian, covered the editorial, highlighting Druckenmiller’s rebuke of his former mentee, Bessent. As the story circulated online, some readers questioned rhetorical choices that resembled AI-generated text.
On Tuesday, Druckenmiller admitted to using the technology.
“I’m not embarrassed by it,” he told Notus.
The Wall Street Journal’s editorial page editor, Paul Gigot, defended Druckenmiller in a statement.
“The question for us is whether what we publish from contributors reflects an author’s original argument, and if the author has the standing and credibility to make it. In Stan Druckenmiller’s case, we have had a relationship with him for many years, and nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion,” Gigot said.
He also called AI “a fact of modern life”.
Druckenmiller further defended the choice in an interview with the Wall Street Journal. “At 73 I’m kind of proud of using it,” he said, also telling the paper: “These are my ideas and I’ve been speaking about them for over 15 years, as anyone who knows me knows. Would I prefer that I was a great writer? Yes, but that’s not who I am.”
Druckenmiller, in his op-ed, opposed the US treasury doubling the size of its government debt buybacks.
The controversy comes as the media industry continues to grapple with its parameters around AI use.
A UC Berkeley math professor came under heat this month for using AI to edit an op-ed in the San Francisco Standard. Zvezdelina Stankova maintained the piece, which argued that test-blind college admissions has resulted in under-prepared students, was the result of “intensive human work”. The Standard said, to their understanding, the piece reflected the “original analysis” of Stankova and her colleagues.
In March, the New York Times cut ties with a freelance journalist, whose use of AI resulted in plagiarism from a Guardian book review. The Times added an editor’s note to the journalist’s book review, noting a violation of its standards.
summary: Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller admitted to using artificial intelligence to help write his recent Wall Street Journal op-ed criticizing former mentee and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. While readers questioned the text's rhetorical style, Druckenmiller and WSJ editors defended the choice, emphasizing that the ideas and opinions were entirely his own. The incident highlights ongoing media industry debates regarding the appropriate use of AI tools in published commentary.
key_points: Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller used AI to write a viral Wall Street Journal op-ed criticizing US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Druckenmiller and WSJ editorial page editor Paul Gigot defended the use of AI, stating the ideas and genuine opinions belonged to Druckenmiller.
Druckenmiller stated he is proud of using the technology at age 73 to help express arguments he has made for over 15 years.
The controversy adds to recent media industry discussions regarding ethical boundaries and standards for AI use in published articles.

title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
author: Emer Moreau
content:
Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
![Getty Images A young woman in a modern office at a table with a co-worker](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/7356/live/324f6630-9fb4-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg.webp) Getty Images
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.
Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.
Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.
However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.
Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.
The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.
Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.
But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.
He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.
From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."
Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.
Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.
The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.
But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.
A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.
"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our £2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."
summary: Figures from the jobs website Adzuna indicate that graduate job vacancies dropped by nearly 50% over the past year to 8,383 in July, reaching the lowest level since tracking began in 2016. Employers are reportedly cutting entry-level roles due to rising costs, such as minimum wage and national insurance hikes, and a shift toward artificial intelligence. While some experts suggest the drop may reflect a change in how jobs are advertised rather than a total market collapse, overall youth unemployment remains a growing concern.
key_points: Graduate vacancies fell from 15,397 last year to 8,383 in July, according to Adzuna data.
Businesses cite rising costs, including minimum wage and national insurance hikes, alongside AI adoption as factors reducing junior roles.
Competition for jobs is increasing, with 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July compared to 1.93 a year earlier.
Some experts note the data may indicate a shift in how graduate positions are advertised rather than a complete market collapse.
Official figures show the UK youth unemployment rate was 16.2% in early 2026, with over one million young people classified as Neet.

title: Labour’s economic vandalism is turning all my friends into unemployed socialists
author: Jack Davey
content:
![A young woman sits indoors with her head bowed and hands clasped to her forehead](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499448404_17875940721870_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqwMpl-Jpdv5EMZZkofEupHOyEA__MmDc0hQxjdbkS2u8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A young woman sits indoors with her head bowed and hands clasped to her forehead](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499448404_17875940721870_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqwMpl-Jpdv5EMZZkofEupHOyEA__MmDc0hQxjdbkS2u8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
It feels like there’s never been a worse time to be a graduate. Despite more students going to university than ever, demand for them in the job market is in free-fall. As The Telegraph reports, just 8,383 graduate roles were advertised in July, a 45 per cent drop on last year. While the Education Secretary, Lucy Powell, brags about “opening doors” for young people, many are finding them firmly closed.
A few months after I graduated in 2024, I didn’t find myself ensconced in a corporate office, eagerly networking with my new colleagues. Instead, I was a day labourer, spending my afternoons staring into a septic tank I was trying to fix. (I even occasionally had to get in.) Despite having moved on from this literal stagnation, I’m still not making as much as when I was in the world of Hebridean waste management.
Britain’s graduate employment market is actually not that different to a faulty sewage system. More people than ever are going into university, but few are managing to get out of it with a job. It’s a blockage that isn’t due to a lack of skills or the failure of higher education; there simply aren’t enough vacancies for Britain’s young talent.
The cause of this is, ironically, the Left-wing policies young people often support. Rachel Reeves’s employers’ National Insurance rise made it far more expensive to hire young workers. This, combined with a stagnant economy, has created huge economic distortions which have not only stopped jobs being created but almost completely eroded the graduate premium on the lower rungs of the corporate ladder. Many of my friends fortunate enough to get a graduate job are earning little more than the minimum wage.
Those are the lucky ones. Others are trapped in stasis: those without connections or a good DEI story and, worst of all, those unlucky enough not to have known what they wanted to do at 18. Every day when they could be gaining experience and progressing is spent cold-emailing or, at best, hopping from one three-month internship to another.
It’s not all bad. Some just assume things will get better. Upper-middle-class people I know are using the money they’ve saved to go travelling and wait things out until their parents can network them into an opportunity. Sadly, most don’t have this option.
It is hard to overstate the effect this stagnation has had on young graduates, even at “prestigious universities”. I have friends with straight A*s and first-class degrees from top-five universities who can’t get past a second-round interview. One recently wondered whether all the reading he had done was not only useless in getting a job but had actively harmed his chances of employment.
Just after I graduated, my fellow humanities students started jumping into law as the only safe port for the world’s last readers. Others looked to teaching or even the police as secure employment. In every field, the fight for employment gets more intense each year, with many battle-hardened after years of underemployment. I know of 26-year-olds and 28-year-olds with years of work on their CVs getting onto graduate schemes for the first time.
Politicians have begun to move away from the plight of graduates to focus on small numbers of prestigious apprenticeships, and on glorifying the “hard hat”. They promote them as high-skill pathways, when the reality is that the most common schemes are in health and social work.
The tragic irony of all this is that, despite their purgatory, Britain’s young have an appetite for their own destruction. I have personal experience of this too. One Left-leaning young lawyer I know told me that, despite the ruinous tax bill coming her way, she “wouldn’t know what to do with the money anyway”. And when the young do rebel, it’s in an even more ruinous direction. A YouGov poll of 18-24 year-olds from the start of the month had the Greens on 43 per cent.
The declining prospects of Britain’s youth are real, and, despite its absurdity, the message from the radical Left that it is all the fault of “the rich” is cutting through. Today’s young revolutionaries might talk about overturning the system, but they are effectively calling for more of the same. Higher taxes, more diversity and more immigration. They don’t just want things to get worse; they want them to get worse faster.
summary: Britain's graduate employment market is facing a severe downturn, with job advertisements dropping significantly compared to the previous year. Left-wing policies, such as Rachel Reeves's employers' National Insurance rise, have made hiring young workers more expensive and contributed to a stagnant economy. Despite facing underemployment and a lack of vacancies, many young people continue to support left-leaning policies and political parties.
key_points: Graduate job advertisements fell by 45 per cent in July compared to the previous year.
Rachel Reeves's employers' National Insurance rise has made hiring young workers much more expensive.
Many graduates are struggling to find work, with some earning little more than the minimum wage or caught in unpaid internships.
High-achieving graduates from top universities are facing intense competition and struggling to secure employment.
Despite poor economic prospects, many young people continue to support left-wing political parties and policies.

title: High street risks collapse without immediate support, Labour warned
author: Szu Ping Chan
content:
![Andy Burnham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499428524_17875795632620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwRcfSI6dlxc0VDfiMWTAIeM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Andy Burnham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499428524_17875795632620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwRcfSI6dlxc0VDfiMWTAIeM.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Andy Burnham will preside over a fresh wave of business closures unless Britain’s high streets receive immediate financial support, bosses have warned.
Mr Burnham has commissioned an independent review into how pubs and hotels pay property taxes, known as business rates.
However, business leaders say the review, to be led by Jerry Schurder, a retail expert, is too narrow and would not report back until 2027 – with recommendations not coming into force until the end of the decade.
Craig Beaumont, from the Federation of Small Businesses, called on Mr Burnham and John Healey to provide more relief at the Budget.
He said: “Business rates have spiked and with high inflationary annual rises on top to come, many small business owners will struggle to keep their business viable.
“At a time of minimal margins and their five big bills rising – rates, rent, energy, staff and tax – something has to give.”
Mr Beaumont said the threshold at which small businesses are exempt from paying business rates had not changed in almost a decade.
This had dragged hundreds of thousands of small firms into paying the tax which raises more than £35bn a year.
Allen Simpson, of UK Hospitality, also called for more help at the Budget to address “immediate financial challenges”.
The lobby group warned that three hospitality businesses were closing every week as a result of Labour’s repeated tax raids.
Mr Simpson said: “While I support the Government’s independent review to improve the system to better reflect trading realities, this must be coupled with fiscal action at the Budget to reduce the entire hospitality sector’s tax burden, of which business rates represent a significant proportion.”
Mr Burnham last month announced a 20pc cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England from April, following The Telegraph’s campaign to save British pubs.
Many have been hit by soaring bills after the Government called time on pandemic-era relief measures and the introduction of new rates to reflect a revaluation.
The move will be funded partly by higher levies on warehouses operated by tech giants such as Amazon.
Mr Burnham has also indicated that he will target owners of vacant high-street properties.
‘Another review just doesn’t cut it’
Andrew Griffith, the shadow business secretary, said the review would make little difference to the current challenges facing business owners.
He said: “Another review – after Labour promised ‘permanently lower business rates’ at the last election – just doesn’t cut it. Too many businesses are heading over the cliff and they need someone to grab the wheel right now, not an inquiry to admire the smoking wreckage in a year’s time!”
Others warned that limiting the review to pubs and hotels would leave businesses in other sectors struggling.
Jonny Haseldine, at the British Chambers of Commerce, said: “While it is welcome for the pubs and hotels we represent, this review of valuations should be wider, and cover every sector. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach.”
James Murray, the financial secretary to the Treasury, said the Government recognised the “vital” contribution of pubs to the economy.
He said: “Last month we announced tax cuts for pubs to give them the breathing room they need. Today we’re going further with a rethink of valuations – so that we can build a fairer system for the future.”
summary: Business leaders have warned that high streets face a collapse without immediate financial support and relief at the upcoming Budget. While Andy Burnham commissioned an independent review into business rates for pubs and hotels, critics argue the scope is too narrow and will take too long to implement. Industry figures point to rising costs, including business rates, rent, energy, staff, and taxes, as key pressures threatening the viability of small businesses and hospitality venues.
key_points: Business leaders warned that high streets risk a fresh wave of closures without immediate financial support.
An independent review on business rates led by Jerry Schurder was criticized for being too narrow and reporting too late.
The Federation of Small Businesses called for urgent relief at the Budget to help firms facing spiked rates and rising operational bills.
UK Hospitality warned that three hospitality businesses close every week due to tax pressures.
Shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith criticized the review, stating that businesses need immediate action rather than an inquiry.

title: Winter energy prices expected to rise to three year high
author: Kevin Peachey
content:
![Woman in floral dress with blonde hair pinned up adjusts heating system in her home](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/b19a/live/2109aba0-a091-11f1-b11c-1bea5fc925f5.jpg)
- Published
Energy bills for millions of households are expected to rise this winter to the highest level for three years, under a price cap to be announced by the industry regulator on Wednesday.
The cap will reflect the rise in the wholesale cost of gas, paid by suppliers and will hit bills just as the colder weather arrives in October until the end of December.
Analysts expect Ofgem to say prices will go up by 4% compared with the current cap, affecting those on variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.
Firms say energy debt has jumped and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay. The government says VAT is being cut from electricity bills.
The price cap for about 33 million households is expected to rise, driven by volatility in international wholesale gas prices.
The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.
Millions of people have moved on to fixed energy tariffs, some in response to the uncertainty created by the impact of the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Anyone on a fixed deal will not see the price they pay rise, until at least the end of the term of their tariff. About 40% of billpayers have fixed tariffs.
![A bar chart showing the energy price cap for a typical household on a price-capped, dual-fuel tariff paying by direct debit, from January 2022 to April 2026. The figure was Â£1,319 based on typical usage in October 2021. This rose to a high of Â£4,414 in January 2023, although the Energy Price Guarantee limited bills to Â£2,500 for a typical household between October 2022 and June 2023. Bills dropped to Â£1,685 in July 2024, before rising slightly to Â£1,846 in October, Â£1,869 in January 2025, Â£1,992 in April 2025, Â£1,854 in July 2025, Â£1,892 in October 2025, Â£1,758 in January 2026, Â£1,641 in April 2026. The cap in July is Â£1,663 under the new typical household consumption values.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/be66/live/922d0330-a074-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
The energy cap sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, not the total bill, so a household's final bill depends on what they use.
In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back owing to high prices of recent years while energy efficiency has improved.
Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.
Cornwall Insight, the consultancy, has forecast that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity, paid through direct debit, will pay Â£1,729 a year from October.
This is up from Â£1,663 between July and September and woild be the highest for three years.
Households are paying hundreds of pounds a year more on average than before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 started the energy crisis. Bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, according to industry data.
That means unpaid bills and charges have shot up. Energy UK estimates total debt to have collectively risen to Â£6bn, with an expectation of it to increase to about Â£7bn by the end of the year.
The average billpayer in debt, without a payment plan, owed Â£3,500, it said.
The trade body has called for a flexible discounted tariff for those most in need, funded by taxation. That is supported by many debt charities.
"Without urgent intervention â namely a national social tariff and implementation of the long-awaited debt write off scheme from Ofgem â we expect this [debt] figure to rise in the coming months, and with that see an increase in the number of people coming to us for help with energy bills," said Emily Whitford, senior public policy advocate at StepChange.
The Trades Union Congress has called for a windfall tax on bank profits to be used to reduce energy bills.
The government is cutting VAT from electricity bills in October, which should knock about Â£50 off a typical annual bill, and some policy costs were cancelled or shifted in April, but ministers say there is more to do.
Suppliers offer a host of support schemes to anyone struggling to pay, or who is likely to find it difficult.
Energy UK has a list of these schemes, external. But it stresses that companies can often only help if you get in touch with your supplier to tell them you are unable to pay.
summary: Energy bills for millions of households across England, Scotland, and Wales are expected to reach a three-year high this winter due to rising wholesale gas prices. Ofgem's upcoming price cap is anticipated to increase by 4% for those on variable tariffs starting in October. In response to mounting energy debt, which Energy UK estimates could reach £7bn by the end of the year, industry groups and charities are calling for targeted financial support and social tariffs.
key_points: Ofgem is expected to announce a 4% increase in the energy price cap for variable tariffs, effective from October to December.
The rise is driven by volatility and increases in international wholesale gas prices.
About 40% of billpayers on fixed tariffs will not experience price increases until their current terms end.
Collective household energy debt has risen significantly, with industry groups calling for government intervention and social tariffs.

title: EMR warns passengers 'may not be able to board' due to strikes
author: Isaac Ashe
content:
![A passenger walking up stairs at St Pancras station](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/799a/live/645ef7c0-a096-11f1-91dc-4919512f173f.jpg)
A queueing system will be in place for EMR passengers at London St Pancras
- Published
East Midlands Railway (EMR) has warned passengers should carry out "essential travel only" over the Bank Holiday due to strike action.
The operator said it will have a "significantly reduced" service on Sunday and Monday, with a queueing system for boarding at London St Pancras and Sheffield. It warned "it may not be possible to board your intended service".
The Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union has been in dispute with EMR since April over the rollout of the Aurora (Class 810 fleet), which it said had operated with a "significant number" of faults.
After industrial action on three Saturdays in August, it announced more strikes while what EMR called "constructive discussions" continued.
EMR previously said "no safety-critical faults have been identified that prevented the trains from meeting regulatory requirements for passenger service".
![The front of a purple East Midlands Railway train on the track](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/9b23/live/3695bd30-9e19-11f1-95e0-53a570c83624.jpg)
The new Aurora (Class 810) trains were brought into service in December 2025
On Sunday and Monday, EMR will run a reduced timetable from around 08:00 to 19:00 BST.
Customers are advised to only travel if their journey is "absolutely essential", allow extra time at stations, and to check their full journey, including first and last trains, before travelling.
It added that on Sunday there will be no LNER trains between London King's Cross and Peterborough as part of digital signalling upgrades being carried out by Network Rail, leading to increased demand.
![Trains lined up on tracks with EMR livery](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/30d6/live/e18b2e20-9d77-11f1-a7fd-5fe2fcb0be12.jpg)
The Rail, Maritime and Transport union has been in dispute with East Midlands Railway since April
Philippa Cresswell, EMR customer experience director, said: "We recognise how frustrating this disruption will be for customers, particularly following the three Saturdays affected by RMT strike action earlier this month, and we are very sorry for the impact this will have on August Bank Holiday plans.
"We continue to have constructive discussions with the RMT and have met with the union six times as we work towards resolving the issues at the heart of this dispute."
Further strikes will take place on 16 and 17 September, RMT said.
EMR reduced services in July due to "reliability issues" with the new Class 810 trains.
Hitachi Rail previously said it had increased its capacity for "modifications and testing", and was working with all partners to resolve the issues.
EMR has since announced it will reinstate some cancelled Intercity services from the end of August.
Listen to BBC Radio Derby on Sounds and follow BBC Derby on Facebook, external, on X, external, or on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk, external or via WhatsApp, external on 0808 100 2210.
summary: East Midlands Railway (EMR) has advised passengers to undertake essential travel only over the Bank Holiday due to upcoming RMT strike action. The operator will run a significantly reduced service and implement queueing systems, warning that travelers may not be able to board their intended trains. The ongoing dispute centers on the rollout and alleged faults of the new Aurora Class 810 fleet.
key_points: EMR warned passengers they may not be able to board trains due to strike action over the Bank Holiday weekend.
A reduced timetable will operate from around 08:00 to 19:00 BST on Sunday and Monday, featuring queueing systems at London St Pancras and Sheffield.
The RMT union dispute with EMR involves concerns over the rollout and faults of the new Aurora (Class 810) train fleet.
Additional RMT strikes are scheduled for 16 and 17 September.
Network Rail digital signalling upgrades halting LNER trains between London King's Cross and Peterborough are expected to increase passenger demand.

title: US consumer confidence falls in August as gas prices remain above $4 per gallon
author: Associated Press; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Americans’ confidence in the economy declined again this month as the ongoing conflict in Iran continued to push US gasoline prices above $4 per gallon.
The Conference Board said on Tuesday that its consumer confidence index dipped to 89.4 in August from 90.2 in July. That was the lowest level in seven months but was essentially within the same lukewarm range it has been in since the beginning of the year. In late 2024 and early 2025, readings were consistently above 100.
Respondents’ views of their present situation improved, but their short-term outlook soured.
Americans remain frustrated with the economy after five years of elevated inflation, potentially posing a risk to Donald Trump and Republicans in the midterm elections, which are fewer than 70 days away.
Write-in responses to the board’s survey, collected from 3 August to 16 August, were slightly more pessimistic this month. References to prices in general – and oil and gas prices specifically – remained elevated. Comments about war and geopolitics, food prices, trade, and jobs rose in August.
Trump continues to blame high prices on his predecessor Joe Biden, yet inflation has risen since Trump’s inauguration last year.
The Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge – the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index – was up 3.7% in June from a year earlier. That was down from May’s 4.1% year-over-year increase but up from 2.8% before the Iran war began on 28 February. It was 2.5% when Trump was inaugurated in January 2025.
The government will issue its July PCE data on Wednesday.
Consumers’ views of the current labor market improved in August, with 27% saying jobs were “plentiful”, up from 24.4% in July. However, respondents were more negative about the labor market over the next six months, with just 14.6% expecting more jobs to be available, down from 16.4% last month.
The US job market stalled unexpectedly in July as employers cut 23,000 jobs. To make matters worse, Department of Labor revisions erased 103,000 jobs from previously reported May and June payrolls.
The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, but for the wrong reason: thousands of people dropped out of the labor market, leaving fewer people competing for work.
summary: US consumer confidence declined to a seven-month low in August as ongoing conflict in Iran kept gasoline prices above $4 per gallon. While views on the present economic and labor situation slightly improved, Americans' short-term outlook soured amid persistent frustration with inflation. This economic discontent could pose a risk to Republicans and Donald Trump in the upcoming midterm elections.
key_points: The Conference Board consumer confidence index fell to 89.4 in August from 90.2 in July.
Gasoline prices remained above $4 per gallon due to the ongoing conflict in Iran.
The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.7% in June from a year earlier.
Consumers' views of the current labor market improved, but expectations for the next six months worsened.

title: Simon Calder: Rail misery this weekend will cap a dismal month for passengers
author: Simon Calder
content:
![LNER Azuma train passing red lights at an unmanned Level crossing, East Coast Main Line Railway, Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, England, UK](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499441996_17875883415561_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![LNER Azuma train passing red lights at an unmanned Level crossing, East Coast Main Line Railway, Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, England, UK](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499441996_17875883415561_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
August, the peak month for leisure train travel in the UK, has been blighted by rail disruption at an unprecedented scale due to derailments and power cuts.
More misery for travellers is to come over the Bank Holiday. For years Network Rail has chosen the last long weekend until Christmas to close some lines for complex engineering projects, and 2026 is no exception – with an emphasis on key north-south routes. But a combination of strikes and schedule reductions will exacerbate the disruption caused by route closures.
As a result, fares on domestic flights are soaring above £1,000 – and even Anglo-Scottish buses have broken the £100 barrier as travellers seek alternatives.
August chaos so far
East Midlands Railway has cut one in eight of its intercity trains linking Sheffield, Derby, Nottingham and Leicester with London St Pancras International due to “ongoing service reliability issues” with the rolling stock.
The first of two power cuts at control centres happened on Aug 6, when a 90-second loss of electricity at a Network Rail hub in Manchester brought the railways to a standstill in north-west England. Hundreds of thousands of rail passengers endured a chaotic rush-hour with disruption continuing into the following day.
![Empty train lines at Hunts Cross railway station in Liverpool, as an electricity supply failure at a communications centre is causing major disruption to trains](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000497577647_17875874269971_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqXgrBd0P19THPvf9738yRPf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Six days later, 30 people were injured – several of them seriously – when a Southern train derailed on the busy London-Eastbourne line. The track north of Lewes will remain closed for the rest of August and possibly beyond.
A second derailment within 24 hours, thankfully without serious injury, closed the line between Shenfield and Southend Victoria in Essex. The earliest that services will be restored is Wednesday, Aug 26.
On Sunday, Aug 23, tens of thousands of rail passengers on CrossCountry were forced to find alternative routes after the firm cancelled almost all of its trains due to a power cut at its control centre. The company, which links England, Wales and Scotland through its hub in Birmingham, vowed to restore services in full on Monday. In fact, there are dozens of cancellations, curtailments and delays due to staff shortage, trains being late from depots and a broken rail near Bristol Parkway.
![People by the departures boards at Bristol Temple Meads train station after CrossCountry train services have been cancelled "across almost all routes" on Sunday following a power cut](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499317672_17875874254350_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqi2ctj82rCJy3QOqq5vOjvf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A spokesman said: “We must now review what measures we need to take to better protect ourselves from the impact of external power outages, for the sake of our customers and the resilience of our operation. We will begin this work straight away.”
Bank Holiday pain for intercity passengers
Britain’s flagship rail route, the East Coast Main Line, will close between London King’s Cross and Peterborough from 10pm on Saturday, Aug 29 until 8am on Monday, Aug 31. The line connects the capital with Yorkshire, north-east England and Scotland. The main operator, LNER, will start and end most trains on Sunday, Aug 30 at Peterborough, with rail-replacement buses to and from Bedford. In addition, a very limited service will run from Newcastle to Bedford, for onward connections to London.
Grand Central is cancelling all trains on Sunday. Lumo is running only between Newcastle and Scotland. Hull Trains will operate a reduced service to and from St Pancras rather than its main hub, London King’s Cross.
Further disruption on diversion routes
Many travellers between Yorkshire and the capital would naturally switch to East Midlands Railway. But members of the RMT union working for the train operator will walk out on Aug 30 and 31 over “ongoing safety concerns and major train faults” connected with the new intercity fleet. This is likely to remove most or all trains from the diversion route, and also reduce the number of services between Bedford and London.
![LNER Azuma service from Berwick upon Tweed to London Kings Cross arrives in platform 3 at York](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/travel/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499441414_17875876929790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Displaced passengers hoping to travel north-south are likely to move to Avanti West Coast or CrossCountry, or both, leading to crowding.
CrossCountry passengers already face disruption due to the closure of the line between Birmingham New Street and Coleshill Parkway right through the weekend. In addition, Avanti West Coast services are reduced due to the closure of the line between Wolverhampton and Stafford on the Sunday of the Bank Holiday.
Workarounds for rail passengers
East Midlands Railway is allowing passengers booked on the strike days, Aug 30 and 31, to travel on either of the two days preceding or following the industrial action.
From London to Edinburgh, air fares on August 30 are looking reasonable, with seats available on easyJet and Ryanair from around £50. But heading southbound at the end of the August festivities in the Scottish capital, the cheapest fare is £110. The British Airways flight at 2pm is selling at £1,222 one way.
Even on FlixBus, the lowest Edinburgh-London fare on any of the six daily direct coaches is £79. The key morning departures are selling at £103 for a journey of over nine hours.
summary: August has seen unprecedented rail disruption in the UK due to power cuts, derailments, and rolling stock issues, with further misery expected over the Bank Holiday weekend. Planned engineering works, combined with upcoming strikes and schedule reductions on key north-south routes, are worsening travel conditions. Consequently, alternatives such as domestic flights and buses have experienced surging prices exceeding £1,000 and £100 respectively.
key_points: August leisure travel has been severely impacted by derailments and control center power cuts.
Network Rail's engineering closures on key north-south routes will coincide with upcoming strikes over the Bank Holiday weekend.
Major operators like East Midlands Railway, LNER, and CrossCountry face extensive cancellations, service reductions, and route closures.
Alternative travel costs have spiked significantly, with domestic flight and long-distance bus fares soaring amid high demand.

title: FTSE 100 Live: Blue-chips dip into the red as Wall Street opens in the green
author: Ephrem Joseph
content:
FTSE 100 Live: Blue-chips dip into the red as Wall Street opens in the green
Last updated: 15:09 25 Aug 2026 BST, First published: 07:15 25 Aug 2026 BST
- FTSE 100 down 14 points at 10,840
- Wall Street opens higher
- Vistry jumps 16% and Melrose rises 9%
- Brent tumbles 3% to around $89.36
- Gold eases but copper advances
- SmallCap and AIM indices move higher
3.09pm: Into the red
The FTSE 100 has slipped into the red mid-afternoon, having bobbed just above the gain line for most of the session.
Standard Chartered leads the retreat, followed by Diageo and Compass, an odd trio given the latter two are usually where money hides when it gets nervous.
Wall Street is having a better time of it.
The Dow and S&P 500 both opened up around 0.4%, with the Nasdaq Composite ahead 0.7% as it shook off Monday's tech slide.
Investors are brushing past new trade measures against Canada and Iran, tonight's Nvidia earnings, and Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole outing as Fed chair.
Oil and bond yields are falling, which helps.
1.20pm: Footsie drifts as Wall Street waits on Warsh, Nvidia and an $80,000 bitcoin
The FTSE 100 was up 11 points in early afternoon trading, which is technically progress, though nobody looks especially committed.
Drifting is the word.
Traders appear content to park up and wait for the Americans, who have rather more on their plate today.
US futures were pointing gently upwards, with Dow and S&P 500 contracts ahead 0.3% and the Nasdaq 100 up 0.7% as it shook off Monday's tech wobble.
Asia was less cheerful, falling broadly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled fresh sanctions on Iran.
Nvidia has now managed seven consecutive down days ahead of tonight's earnings, which is quite the warm-up act for the most-watched results in the market.
Bitcoin, meanwhile, is ignoring the gloom entirely, vaulting above $80,000 for the first time in three months as Treasury intervention in the bond market revived dollar debasement chatter.
Gold rallied too, then stopped for a breather.
Over in retail, Dick's Sporting Goods slumped 14% before the bell after missing second-quarter forecasts and slashing full-year earnings guidance to as little as $10.94 a share.
New home sales, ADP employment and manufacturing data land later, ahead of tomorrow's inflation print and Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole debut as Fed chair.
11.45am: Mid-cap rally strengthens as oil stocks retreat
The FTSE 250 climbed 0.6% to 24,862, close to its session high, while the FTSE 100 added 0.2% to 10,872.
Vistry led the mid-cap market with a 16.3% gain following its £350 million government funding award. Goodwin advanced 8.1%, while PPHE Hotel Group and Jupiter Fund Management rose more than 4%.
Melrose remained the leading FTSE 100 performer, up 9.4%. Rightmove and Marks & Spencer gained around 2.8%, while Next, Rolls-Royce and IAG also advanced.
Diageo fell 1.7%, with London Stock Exchange Group and Endeavour Mining down more than 1%.
Gold eased 0.3% to around $4,636 an ounce but remained close to a three-month high. Endeavour Mining, Fresnillo and Hochschild Mining retreated, while copper rose 0.5% to $6.64 per pound.
Brent crude dropped 3% to approximately $89.36 a barrel as Washington’s Iran sanctions proved less severe than markets had feared and signs of possible diplomatic progress reduced immediate supply concerns. BP fell 0.3% and Shell declined 0.4%.
The FTSE SmallCap gained 0.4%, although none of its constituents rose more than 12%. The AIM All-Share added 0.2%, with Mothercare, Galileo Resources, Futura Medical, Tungsten West, Proteome Sciences and Haydale all gaining more than 12%.
Bitcoin traded near $79,245, up 1.9% but below its intraday high of $81,104.
10.10 am: FTSE 250 pulls ahead as sector leadership broadens
The FTSE 100 was up around 10 points at 10,865, having touched 10,886, while the FTSE 250 strengthened 0.4% to approximately 24,814.
The FTSE SmallCap gained about 0.2%, while the AIM All-Share was broadly flat.
Industrials remained the strongest blue-chip sector. Melrose led the FTSE 100 with an 8.7% gain, while Rolls-Royce, Halma, Weir Group and IMI also advanced.
Housebuilders strengthened across both indices. Persimmon, Taylor Wimpey, Barratt Redrow and Berkeley Group rose, while FTSE 250 constituent Vistry jumped 16.7% to 313.4p after reaching 320.6p.
Retail and financial shares also provided support. Next gained almost 2%, while Legal & General, Aviva, Lloyds, Barclays and Standard Chartered traded higher.
Mining shares remained mixed as gold fell 0.5% to around $4,630 an ounce and copper eased 0.2% to $6.59 per pound. Anglo American gained 0.7%, but Endeavour Mining, Fresnillo, Antofagasta and Hochschild Mining declined.
Energy stocks were slightly weaker as Brent crude dropped 1.4% to approximately US$90.90. BP and Shell both edged lower.
Away from the leading indices, small caps Volex, Galileo Resources, Futura Medical, Mothercare and Tungsten West made serious gains during the session.
Galileo’s 22% rise followed the identification of a potentially substantial copper porphyry system at its Ferber project in Nevada. Tungsten West gained around 16% after securing up to £71 million of government backing for the Hemerdon mine. Mothercare and Futura Medical had no fresh regulatory announcement supporting their moves.
Petra Diamonds was around 13% higher, although the rise occurred on very thin trading volume.
Bitcoin traded near $79,700, up 3.3%, after reaching US$81,104.
9.10 am: Mining rally fades as London edges higher
The FTSE 100 gained 13 points to 10,867 after reaching 10,883, while the FTSE 250, FTSE SmallCap and AIM All-Share also edged higher.
Gold traded around US$4,630 an ounce after approaching US$4,700 earlier. Bullion is up about 13.5% during August and remains on course for its strongest monthly gain since 1999.
However, yesterday’s mining rally has not continued. Endeavour Mining fell 1.6%, Fresnillo lost around 1% and Antofagasta slipped 0.4%. Anglo American gained 0.4%, while Glencore and Rio Tinto were broadly unchanged.
Instead, company announcements produced the largest moves. Volex jumped almost 20% to around 640p after reporting strong organic growth and forecasting annual profit ahead of expectations.
FTSE 250 housebuilder Vistry climbed about 14% following a £350 million funding award to deliver more than 3,000 affordable homes.
On AIM, Tungsten West gained nearly 14% after securing up to £71 million of National Wealth Fund backing for the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine.
Melrose remained the leading FTSE 100 riser, advancing more than 8%, while Next and Rolls-Royce also gained.
