Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, had £23.6bn of headroom against her fiscal targets in the spring. But this is estimated to have fallen as low as £8bn because of inflation and rising borrowing costs, according to the Resolution Foundation.
It adds to the challenge facing Mr Burnham and Mr Healey, whose new Government has pledged to tackle the cost of living while grappling with constrained public finances.
Welfare spending is already on track to hit £353bn, up from £314bn when Labour entered Downing Street in 2024.
A Treasury spokesman said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security.
“The Chancellor and Prime Minister are in lockstep that the Government will meet the fiscal rules, with a buffer against uncertainty – and that includes getting debt down.
“We’re cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 economy to the lowest level in six years.”
summary: The Institute for Fiscal Studies has warned that persistent high inflation, driven partly by conflict in the Middle East, could add an extra £1.7bn to Britain's benefits bill and up to £4.7bn in total to government spending. Price rises are also expected to increase costs for public sector pensions and debt interest, putting severe pressure on the Chancellor ahead of the Budget. Economists predict inflation will climb further in the coming months, eroding the value of department budgets and shrinking fiscal headroom.
key_points: Britain's benefits bill could rise by an extra £1.7bn if inflation remains at 2.9pc into the autumn.
Higher inflation could increase total government spending by up to £4.7bn, including public sector pensions and debt interest.
Ofgem is expected to announce that typical gas and electricity bills will rise by 4pc in October to £1,729.
Inflation is projected by economists to breach 3pc and potentially climb to 3.5pc by the end of the year.
The Chancellor's fiscal headroom has reportedly shrunk from £23.6bn down to as low as £8bn due to inflation and rising borrowing costs.

title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
author: Christopher Jasper
content:
![Computer generated picture of a Virgin train at St Pancras International station](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000498685114_17875728024660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqc_R-fZbnPPOo5bCoTTw0OuLUFsZY-6ahzSUzVgifUsg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Computer generated picture of a Virgin train at St Pancras International station](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000498685114_17875728024660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqc_R-fZbnPPOo5bCoTTw0OuLUFsZY-6ahzSUzVgifUsg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.
Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.
But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.
Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.
However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.
![Sir Richard Branson at St Pancras International station](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000446904194_17874815595350_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqaxc0yOCWITeJw1uajCk_kGWo-KAdI1N_TSsvo9Yxjxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.
Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.
If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.
Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.
Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.
Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.
“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.
“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”
Customer service front and centre
Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.
A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”
On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.
Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.
Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.
That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.
The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.
Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.
“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”
![An aerial photograph shows the Temple Mills International train depot](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000487194674_17874818774400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqadu-bubCwwNTr_YiFtRU6zzhxYwwKH5sUws766CzosU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
No room for slippage
However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.
Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.
Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.
Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.
Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.
It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.
Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.
According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.
He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”
summary: Sir Richard Branson's Virgin Trains has secured permission from Britain's rail regulator to run 20 daily trains between London and the Continent, aiming to challenge Eurostar's 31-year monopoly. The ambitious venture plans to introduce a customer-focused service starting with London-to-Paris routes by October 2030, potentially lowering ticket prices and expanding international rail options. However, Virgin still faces hurdles, including negotiating access to the Channel tunnel and foreign tracks, as well as awaiting delivery of untested Alstom trains.
key_points: Virgin Trains secured regulatory approval from the ORR to operate 20 trains a day between London and the Continent.
The new service plans to launch in October 2030 with routes to Paris, followed by Brussels and Amsterdam.
Competition from Virgin and other operators like Trenitalia could potentially lower ticket prices by nearly a third.
Virgin has ordered 12 untested high-speed single-decker trains from Alstom to support its premium service offering.

title: Nvidia’s mounting debt pile alarms traders
author: Chris Price
content:
That is despite Wall Street estimates that Nvidia’s revenues will nearly double when it reports its next set of quarterly results on Wednesday. Analysts believe the $5.2tn (£3.8tn) company’s sales will top $92bn.
Nvidia’s swap prices have soared on the back of a series of complex financing deals intended to pay for trillions of dollars in AI data centres.
The company’s debt levels jumped this summer after it raised $25bn in its largest-ever bond-market fundraising in June.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, announced $500bn of AI financing deals this month with six Wall Street giants, which would see the lenders create special funding vehicles to back large data centres.
Nvidia confirmed last week that it had agreed to backstop a large US data centre being built by OpenAI with up to $105bn in credit support. It has also announced a $500bn deal with South Korean memory chip giant SK Hynix.
Michael Burry, the US investor depicted in the film The Big Short, has claimed that some of Nvidia’s debt deals are “unnatural” and a kind of “circular” financing.
Costs for insuring debt have soared across the technology industry. Swap prices for other infrastructure giants, including Oracle and Broadcom, have also risen to record levels.
Patrick Perret-Green, the chief executive of advisory firm PPG Macro, said the CDS prices were “quite remarkable” given the apparent strength of the industry.
Benedict Keim, a portfolio manager at Altana Wealth, said investors were increasingly watching the “strong correlation” between Nvidia and the wider AI sector, which is heavily loss-making and has been fuelled by borrowing.
He added that the “vast scale” of the credit guarantees that Nvidia was offering to other AI labs had “increased concerns over its future cash flow and credit risk”.
There are also concerns over Nvidia’s role in allegedly circular financing deals. These risked creating “cascading losses through the ecosystem and increasing the probability of systemic risks in the future”, Mr Keim said.
Amish Patel, the head of equity research at Raymond James, added: “The rise in Nvidia’s CDS reflects growing scrutiny of the company’s expanding role in financing the AI ecosystem.”
Nvidia is considering investing in AI start-up Perplexity, which The Information values at $30bn.
Nvidia was contacted for comment.
summary: Nvidia's mounting debt and complex financing deals for AI data centres have raised concerns among traders and analysts despite expectations of surging revenues. The company recently raised $25bn in bond-market fundraising and announced massive AI financing agreements, including credit support for OpenAI. This heavy borrowing and use of credit guarantees have driven up debt-insuring swap prices and sparked fears of potential systemic risks and future credit strain.
key_points: Nvidia raised $25bn in its largest-ever bond-market fundraising in June.
CEO Jensen Huang announced $500bn in AI financing deals with Wall Street lenders.
Nvidia agreed to provide up to $105bn in credit support for an OpenAI data centre.
Investors and analysts have raised concerns over circular financing and potential systemic risks.

title: Thames Water creditors accused of ‘shuffling chairs on Titanic’ with plan for new board
author: Alex Daniel
content:
The group of creditors pursuing a rescue bid for Thames Water have been accused of shuffling the deckchairs on the Titanic after proposing an overhaul of the stricken utility’s board.
In a bid to stave off temporary nationalisation by Andy Burnham, the lenders said they would appoint Liz Barber, the former chief executive of Yorkshire Water, and Clive Selley, the former chief executive of network operator Openreach, as directors if they are allowed to take formal control of the company.
London & Valley Water (L&VW), a consortium of 100 institutional investors holding £17bn of the company’s £21bn debt, has also lined up Dame Bernadette Kelly, the former permanent secretary of the Department for Transport.
Mike McTighe, the corporate troubleshooter leading Thames’s overhaul, would become the new chair, replacing the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if Thames is able to get its £10bn rescue deal approved by the government. McTighe is the current chair of Openreach.
He said: “The challenge at Thames Water is huge. If this recapitalisation plan is accepted, we will apply full dedication as a new board, working alongside the executive team to transform the business and build a culture in which the customers and local communities who depend on Thames Water come first.”
The proposed appointments are designed to reassure the government that any commercial deal would bring with it a leadership overhaul, as Burnham’s team examines the possibility of taking the company back into public ownership.
L&VW’s announcement was criticised by the public ownership campaign group We Own It. Cat Hobbs, the director at We Own It, said: “This is absolutely absurd. A cosy stitch-up that has nothing to do with the interests of the 16 million people who depend on Thames Water. This amounts to nothing more than a reshuffling of chairs on the deck of the Titanic.”
Burnham has said there should be “greater public control” of Thames Water and previously told the Guardian this could mean nationalisation. This would probably come via placing the company into a special administration regime (SAR), a form of temporary nationalisation.
More recently the prime minister said he was “angry” after companies including Thames Water were given the green light to raise bills even higher earlier this month.
He said the companies must not be allowed to treat bill payers like a “blank cheque”, an escalation of his warnings to utility companies that he is looking at options for more government control of the sector.
The SAR proposal would transfer the costs of running the company to the taxpayer, with Thames Water claiming the bill could come to £2bn.
L&VW, which includes fund managers such as Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital, has also moved to strengthen its legal position in order to be prepared if Thames is nationalised.
after newsletter promotion
The consortium has hired the top litigation and disputes lawyers Pallas Partners to work alongside Akin Gump, the law firm advising the consortium on the terms of their restructuring proposals.
The lenders have been trying to take ownership and bring Thames out of administration after a failed attempt to sell the utility to the US investment group KKR last year.
However, the creditors’ plans were thrown into doubt in June when Emma Reynolds, the then environment secretary, wrote to the regulator, Ofwat, voicing concerns about the terms of the deal.
McTighe said the 10-year plan to turn the water company around would “fix the foundations” at Thames. “It will take time to fix Thames Water, but we are committed to rebuilding trust with the customers and public Thames Water serves,” he said.
Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell, said of the proposed new appointments: “The hope being that these are the sort of credible names which can inspire confidence in the company’s future in private hands.
“Such an outcome would impose large losses on creditors, who are seeking to formally take ownership of the business, having already assumed de facto control, with plans to list it on the stock market as early as 2030.”
summary: Creditors attempting a rescue bid for Thames Water have proposed a leadership overhaul to prevent temporary nationalisation. The consortium, London & Valley Water, has named figures including former Yorkshire Water chief executive Liz Barber and Mike McTighe for new board roles. However, public ownership campaigners criticised the plan as a superficial move, while the government continues to weigh options for increased public control.
key_points: A consortium of creditors holding £17bn of Thames Water's debt has proposed a new board, including Mike McTighe as chair and former Yorkshire Water CEO Liz Barber as a director.
The proposed leadership overhaul aims to reassure the government and stave off temporary nationalisation via a special administration regime.
Campaign group We Own It criticised the plan as an absurd "cosy stitch-up" and likened it to shuffling chairs on the Titanic.
The prime minister has warned that utility companies must not treat bill payers like a blank cheque amid ongoing scrutiny of the sector.

title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
author: Emer Moreau
content:
![A young woman in a modern office at a table with a co-worker](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/7356/live/324f6630-9fb4-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Adzuna said the number of graduate vacancies was the lowest since it started recording in 2016
- Published
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.
Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.
Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.
Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.
The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.
Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.
Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.
Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.
They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.
Many university graduates also face mounting student debt.
Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.
The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.
But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.
summary: According to data from the jobs website Adzuna, graduate job vacancies have fallen by nearly 50% over the past year to the lowest level since records began in 2016. Employers are cutting entry-level roles and turning to artificial intelligence amid rising costs driven by national insurance and minimum wage hikes. Meanwhile, overall competition for jobs is rising, and the UK's youth unemployment rate reached 16.2% in the three months leading to March 2026.
key_points: Graduate vacancies dropped to 8,383 in July, down from 15,397 the previous year.
Rising hiring costs, including minimum wage and national insurance hikes, have contributed to employers cutting junior roles.
Competition among job seekers increased to an average of 2.14 applicants per vacancy in July.
Official figures indicate the UK youth unemployment rate was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026.
While graduate, healthcare, and hospitality vacancies fell, roles in travel, teaching, and construction saw increases.

title: The AI reckoning is coming, it’s just a matter of timing
author: Andrew Orlowski
content:
![Michael Burry at the "The Big Short" New York premiere](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000345979051_17874868656200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq0quQUhCPHdUHY_XWT5Ck7ziIXdNr9atEw2H4ySp7WWI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Michael Burry at the "The Big Short" New York premiere](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000345979051_17874868656200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq0quQUhCPHdUHY_XWT5Ck7ziIXdNr9atEw2H4ySp7WWI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Timing is everything, and fortunes can be made or lost predicting when a bubble will burst.
In 2005, the contrarian hedge fund boss Michael Burry bet against the US mortgage market. Incontinent lenders had approved mortgages to people with little or no income, and had even extended the credit, rolling up the interest into the principal balance. The lenders then sold on these mortgages, which were obscured by securitisation.
But Burry had to wait. As one account put it, he “needed to lay his chips on the table now and wait for the casino to wake up and change the odds of the game”.
It was obvious in hindsight that a small change in the cost of these loans, or the loanees’ ability to pay them, would change things. But it didn’t very much, and as months turned into years, Burry almost lost the lot. However, a reckoning can only be delayed so long. Ultimately a rotten superstructure is maintained only by confidence, and when this evaporates the edifice collapses overnight.
Burry has bet against the AI bubble, and once again he must wait. A staggering proportion of the stock market’s rise since 2022 comes from AI-related companies. While this year’s decline has caught out reckless, quasi-religious believers in AI such as the 24-year old Leopold Aschenbrenner, whose hedge fund collapsed from $45bn to $10bn (£33bn to £7bn) because he bet on the market only going up, it hasn’t become a full-blown rout.
The conventional wisdom is that one company at the centre of the bubble remains relatively impregnable: Nvidia. For the past two years Nvidia has swapped places with Apple as the world’s most valuable company, valued at around $5tn. Nvidia makes the most advanced microprocessors in the world, allowing AI to do more things faster, and it can charge a premium for this valuable product.
Nvidia benefits from the “picks and shovels” idiom. Which is to say that in a gold rush, the smartest investment is in the people who sell mining equipment to the gold prospectors. It doesn’t matter if nobody finds gold. The names on the AI model leadership boards may rise and fall, and favourites may come in and fall out of fashion, but everyone in AI needs Nvidia’s chips to produce the best benchmark results.
Its strength looks even more impregnable considering the difficulties AI model companies like Anthropic or OpenAI are experiencing in building a “competitive moat”. Features are rapidly copied by cheap, open rivals which businesses can run at a much lower cost. Billions spent on R&D almost instantly vanish.
Burry isn’t buying it. He’s short on Nvidia, and last week identified a new Achilles heel. A startup chip rival called Etched he says can produce “10x the performance at lower cost per die” – the manufacturing cost to produce a single functional microchip.
Venture capital is pouring into semiconductor companies that address what is called the “inference bottleneck”, the calculations performed after you’ve sent your prompt. This column has highlighted a few, including British companies Fractile and Olix.
Another was touted by the bullish AI pundit Andrew Côté last week. This is particularly intriguing, as it relates to a classic ploy used by computer companies from IBM to Microsoft to create an impregnable defence: compatibility.
To deter competition, back in the mainframe era, IBM was able to design the socket interfaces by which rivals could attach their own equipment. Those that succeeded, like the company Amdahl, were deemed “plug compatible”.
In the software era, Microsoft defined and controlled the application programming interfaces (APIs), which are really plugs and sockets into the software platform beneath, on which applications are built. Microsoft could easily move the goalposts too, and application developers who were wary of the risk of things breaking chose to stick with Microsoft, even when cheaper alternatives arose.
Nvidia’s great strength today derives from such a socket interface or API called CUDA. For developers who build AI models and applications, CUDA is the only game in town, and for two decades tools have been built on top of that interface.
It’s notable that China, which is desperate for the latest Nvidia chips despite a US embargo, nevertheless forbids its developers from using CUDA. It doesn’t want them getting hooked.
AI infrastructure agent Infinity is using teams of AI agents to optimise models on specific hardware, a job that was simply not worth attempting using expert human labour, but that can yield performance results. CUDA may be made redundant.
Nvidia’s financial strength has been used to finance the data centre build out, which Burry doesn’t like one bit.
According to The Economist, the data centre splurge requires $2.5tn in annual AI revenue to break even. The more sceptical former IMF and Goldman Sachs analyst Peter Berezin believes even $10tn may be low.
Both agree demand can’t match the investment. The big experiments on agentic AI have not worked out, as it is too unreliable. While AI waits for the lucrative mass-market applications investors need, those data centres are depreciating rapidly, and innovations identified by Burry and Côté could render them expensive stranded assets.
Of course, Burry has been wrong before, but was he definitively wrong, or just too early? As John Maynard Keynes warned, the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.
summary: Hedge fund manager Michael Burry has placed a short bet against the current artificial intelligence boom, drawing parallels to his famous 2005 bet against the US mortgage market. While companies like Nvidia have dominated the market by supplying essential microprocessors and dominating software interfaces like CUDA, critics argue that massive data centre investments will struggle to break even. Emerging chip rivals, changing industry standards, and the high costs of infrastructure could threaten Nvidia's stronghold and trigger an AI market correction.
key_points: Michael Burry has bet against the AI bubble, echoing his contrarian short against the US mortgage market in 2005.
Nvidia's high valuation is supported by its advanced microprocessors and its dominant software interface, CUDA.
Data centre build-outs require trillions in annual AI revenue to break even, raising concerns about overinvestment and stranded assets.
Emerging startup chip rivals and alternative optimization technologies threaten to undermine Nvidia's market dominance and render current infrastructure obsolete.

title: New Fed chair faces critical test at Jackson Hole as inflation fears mount
author: Richard Partington
content:
The new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, faces a critical test this week amid anxiety in government bond markets over inflation and Donald Trump’s tax and spending plans.
As the world’s most powerful central bank prepares for its annual Jackson Hole conference, analysts said bond traders would be looking for signals from Warsh over its commitment to fighting inflation.
The Trump-appointed head of the US central bank has previously signalled reluctance to “spoon-feed” financial markets over how it plans to set interest rates to keep fast-rising prices in check.
However, anxiety over Trump’s handling of the economy and investor fears that his war with Iran is stoking inflation have rocked global financial markets amid a dramatic sell-off in US government bonds.
Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at the stockbroker AJ Bell, said: “Investors will be looking for a comfort blanket when Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh addresses the Jackson Hole meeting.”
James Smith, an economist at ING Bank, said: “By offering less commentary on where rates are headed … [Warsh] risks injecting yet more volatility into an already febrile bond market.”
![Kevin Warsh holds a press conference in Washington in June](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1a12d41b92a888edac1a634645fd82b0cd1c0e9e/0_0_3138_2092/master/3138.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Warsh is expected to give a highly anticipated speech on Friday at the Fed’s annual symposium in the Rocky Mountains resort of Jackson Hole, against a volatile backdrop in global financial markets.
The gathering of the world’s most powerful central bankers in the Grand Teton national park is a blue riband event in the financial calendar, as a vital platform for the Fed chair and other top officials to signal their policymaking approach.
However, Warsh has signalled reluctance to use his speech for the “more traditional setup” of dropping hints over how the US central bank may respond to inflationary pressures when its officials next meet to set interest rates in September and December. Instead, he has said his Jackson Hole speech could be “focused on bigger questions”, including concerns over productivity and demographics.
However, the meeting comes as selling pressure intensifies in the $30tn (£22tn) US government debt market despite efforts by the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, to assuage investor worries after he committed to at least double Washington’s purchases of US Treasury bonds.
With investors fretting over the inflationary impact of the Iran war and the US national debt surpassing $40tn for the first time, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on long-term US Treasury debt at first fell, before rising back towards the highest levels since 2007.
after newsletter promotion
Warsh was accused by investors of sending confusing signals in his first press conference as Fed chair in July, after he expressed his commitment to curbing inflation without giving details.
The Fed held rates in July, and trading in financial markets reflects investor expectations for a hold again in September, although a rise is thought possible. Markets anticipate at least one, and possibly two, quarter-point increases by the middle of next year.
Trump, who appointed Warsh, has called on the Fed to cut rates, fuelling investor concerns over interference at the central bank.
Stephen Brown, an economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, said Warsh maintaining a tight-lipped approach could be risky. “He might even stick to the official subject of the symposium, ‘Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy’, in which case his speech could be something of a snoozefest.
“That said, even that approach would risk giving the impression that Warsh is not taking inflation risks seriously, so there could still be volatility in markets.”
summary: New US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh faces a critical test at the Jackson Hole symposium amid mounting investor anxiety over inflation, national debt, and Donald Trump's tax and spending plans. Global financial markets and bond traders are seeking clear signals on interest rates and the Fed's commitment to fighting inflation. However, Warsh has indicated a reluctance to offer traditional hints about near-term rate decisions, choosing instead to focus his upcoming speech on broader questions like productivity and demographics.
key_points: Kevin Warsh faces a critical test at the annual Jackson Hole conference amid bond market volatility.
Investors are anxious over US inflation, national debt surpassing $40tn, and the economic impact of the Iran war.
Warsh has signaled a reluctance to provide traditional hints about upcoming interest rate decisions.
Donald Trump, who appointed Warsh, has pressured the Fed to cut rates, raising concerns over central bank independence.

title: UK graduate job vacancies plunge to lowest in a decade
author: Alex Daniel
content:
Graduate job vacancies in the UK have sunk to their lowest level since they started being tracked a decade ago, according to a recruiting website.
Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, Adzuna reported on Monday, down 45% compared with the same point last year and the lowest since the company started gathering the data in 2016.
The number comes as 262,820 people prepare to go to university in September, a record high that underlines the tough conditions facing graduates entering the job market as entry-level roles are threatened by AI.
About 1 million young people in the UK were not in education, employment or training, otherwise known as Neets, in the first quarter of this year, according to the Office for National Statistics.
Adzuna said sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies, adding that the figures suggested that a recovery reported during the spring had gone into reverse.
Andrew Hunter, a co-founder of Adzuna, said: “July’s numbers are a step backwards, not a blip. The annual vacancy decline got worse for the first time since January, and (the number of) jobseekers per vacancy are now higher than they were a year ago.
“The graduate job market also keeps setting new lows, which tells us employers still haven’t found a reason to open up hiring at that level.”
The figures point to a sharp worsening in the graduate market compared with a decade ago. In 2017, there were more than 55,000 graduate positions.
More recently, employers have also reined in their hiring in the face of increases in national insurance contributions and the minimum wage announced by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in her last two budgets.
The extra labour cost for businesses also comes as some companies are prioritising investment in automation and artificial intelligence tools rather than hiring.
after newsletter promotion
The trend has left some young people increasingly demoralised. One report, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), said this summer that 16- to 21-year-olds were less confident about being successful than a decade ago and that some were “losing faith in their futures”.
In July, Andy Burnham said he would try to boost youth employment with more backing for technical education and apprenticeships.
The only sectors showing increases in jobs for university leavers were travel, teaching and construction, Adzuna said.
Hunter added: “It isn’t all bad news. Teaching, travel, and trade and construction are still adding roles, and manufacturing is now doing the same, too. But that’s a short list, and everyone outside of these sectors is having a harder time than they were three months ago.”
summary: UK graduate job vacancies have fallen to their lowest level in a decade, with just 8,383 roles advertised in July according to recruiting website Adzuna. This 45% drop compared to the previous year coincides with a record number of students preparing to enter university and increased economic pressures on businesses. While sectors like healthcare, hospitality, and logistics saw declines, travel, teaching, construction, and manufacturing continued to add roles.
key_points: Graduate job vacancies dropped to 8,383 in July, the lowest since Adzuna began tracking data in 2016.
The downturn is driven by factors including higher labour costs, increased minimum wage, and companies prioritising AI and automation.
A record 262,820 people are preparing to enter university, facing an increasingly difficult entry-level job market.
Only a few sectors, including travel, teaching, construction, and manufacturing, are still increasing graduate roles.

title: Government vows to make business rate valuations for pubs and hotels fairer
author: Lauren Almeida
content:
The government has promised that business rate valuations will be “made fairer” for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, as Andy Burnham faces growing calls to help the UK’s struggling hospitality sector.
An independent review for England and Wales will look at improving the system for hospitality venues, which were hit by higher business rate bills this year after the end of pandemic-era relief and when new revaluations took effect.
It comes after Burnham announced last month that he would cut business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England by 20% from April next year.
The government has faced calls to reduce the tax burden on hospitality businesses, which have also struggled to cope with rising energy and food bills in recent years.
The review, which will be led by Jerry Schurder, an independent business rates specialist, will report back to the Treasury by the end of March 2027. It will consider valuations before the next revaluation date in 2029. The rise in valuations this year will not be affected.
James Murray, the financial secretary to the Treasury, said: “Pubs and hotels are vital for communities and bringing growth to every postcode,” adding that a “rethink of valuations” would help “build a fairer system for the future”.
Allen Simpson, the chief executive of the trade body UKHospitality, said it was positive the government was looking seriously at the valuation methodology for pubs and hotels.
“Business rates remain a significant burden for hospitality businesses, and the system needs to better reflect the trading realities for the sector,” he said.
Emma McClarkin, the chief executive of the British Beer & Pub Association, said the review was “sorely needed and hugely welcome” as pubs had for years “paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open”.
While cuts have been welcomed by business owners, the industry has repeatedly called for the reform of the whole business rates system. Estimates suggest that two pubs are closing a day across Britain this year, hit by higher taxes, wages, energy and food costs.
after newsletter promotion
Burnham is also facing calls to extend the business rates relief aimed at pubs, clubs and live music venues to bookshops. This month 234 independent booksellers signed an open letter calling on the prime minister to give bookshops the same consideration as other businesses that play a positive role in their communities.
The government has suggested that it will reform business rates, including small business rates relief, at John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.
summary: The UK government has promised an independent review to make business rate valuations fairer for pubs and hotels in England and Wales. Led by Jerry Schurder, the review will report to the Treasury by March 2027 ahead of the 2029 revaluation. The hospitality sector has faced heavy criticism over high business rates, rising energy costs, and closures.
key_points: An independent review will examine business rate valuations for pubs and hotels in England and Wales.
The review will be led by Jerry Schurder and will report to the Treasury by the end of March 2027.
The hospitality sector has struggled with higher business rate bills, rising energy costs, and increased food prices.
Industry trade bodies like UKHospitality and the British Beer & Pub Association welcomed the review.
Independent booksellers have also called on the government for similar business rates relief.

title: Fast-fashion giant Shein aims for $27bn valuation in Hong Kong market debut
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
Shein will debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on 1 September, the fast-fashion retailer said on Monday, in a long-awaited listing that would value the group at close to $27bn.
Founded in China and now headquartered in Singapore, the online retailer secured Beijing’s approval last month to make its initial public offering in Hong Kong.
Its valuation has dropped by about 70% from a near $100bn private market peak four years ago, as it aims to raise up to HK$13.86bn ($1.77bn) in its Hong Kong IPO launched on Monday.
Shein is selling 280m shares between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50 per share, the filings showed, valuing it at close to $27bn at the top of that range. The company will announce the final price on 31 August and start trading on 1 September. With the funds raised from the market, Shein said it aims to finance its technological capabilities as well as boost its international presence.
Known for selling $5 dresses and $10 jeans to shoppers in about 160 countries, the marked decline in valuation comes after Shein faced questions over slowing growth, rising costs and changing market conditions.
Plans to list in New York and London had been held back in recent years by regulatory hurdles, according to media reports.
The firm moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, a move analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.
But it still benefits from China’s unique combination of a huge, low-cost textile manufacturing sector and a highly sophisticated e-commerce logistics network.
By the end of last year, its European customer base rose to 156 million average monthly users, making Shein one of the continent’s biggest e-commerce platforms alongside China’s AliExpress (193 million users) and Amazon (about 180 million users).
In November, the group made waves with its first-ever physical outlet, a dedicated space in the storied BHV department store in Paris.
Hundreds of customers lined up on its opening day, and dozens more people gathered to protest, requiring a heavy police presence to keep the tense situation from getting out of hand.
Demonstrators slammed what they alleged were inhumane working conditions at Shein’s suppliers, the environmental costs of selling clothes not made to last, and unfair competition against brick-and-mortar retailers struggling to stay open.
The company says it holds its suppliers to strict compliance standards and does not tolerate forced labour.
Shein also drew criticism last year in France over the discovery of childlike sex dolls on its platform. The company pledged to cooperate with French authorities and announced it was banning all sex dolls on its platform.
In June, French authorities imposed two fines on Shein totalling more than 22m euros ($25.1m), citing problems with product traceability, environmental labelling and delivery times. At the time Shein said it would contest the “disproportionate” penalties, arguing that no consumer harm had been established.
Overall, Shein has paid over 210m euros in various French fines over the years, and Italy has also imposed fines alleging misleading environmental claims.
Reuters and Agence-France Presse contributed to this report
summary: Fast-fashion retailer Shein plans to debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on September 1, aiming to raise up to $1.77bn in an IPO that would value the company at close to $27bn. This valuation reflects a significant drop from its previous $100bn peak four years ago amid slowing growth, rising costs, and regulatory hurdles. The company intends to use the funds to finance its technological capabilities and boost its international presence, despite facing ongoing controversies, protests, and regulatory fines in Europe over labor, environmental, and product issues.
key_points: Shein is launching its Hong Kong IPO to raise up to HK$13.86bn ($1.77bn) with a target valuation of nearly $27bn.
Trading is scheduled to begin on September 1, following a final price announcement on August 31.
The current valuation is about 70% lower than its peak of nearly $100bn four years ago.
Shein plans to use the raised funds to finance technological capabilities and expand its international presence.
The company has faced numerous challenges in Europe, including protests, regulatory fines, and scrutiny over environmental and labor practices.

title: Graduates face worst jobs market on record
author: Tim Wallace
content:
Graduates are facing the worst job market on record as vacancies evaporate under pressure from tax and technology.
Just 8,383 roles for university leavers were advertised in July, a 45pc drop on a year ago and the lowest since the figures were first compiled in 2016.
The graduate jobs drought contrasts with the record flood of 262,820 18-year-olds preparing to begin their degree studies after earning a university place in their A-level results this month.
It represents a steep challenge to Andy Burnham as rising unemployment and benefits bills limit his options. Meanwhile anger over crippling student debts and the decline in the relative value of a degree is gripping graduates whose Labour votes he will need.
Employers are slashing entry-level hiring after Labour increased National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage, making inexperienced staff less attractive.
At the same time, large employers such as the Big Four accountants are seeking to use AI software to do paperwork that would have traditionally occupied their graduates.
The average graduate salary was advertised at £25,813 last month, roughly equivalent to a full-time job on the minimum wage of £12.71 per hour.
Job prospects for university leavers have sharply deteriorated in the past decade, according to findings by Adzuna, a recruitment website. From a peak of more than 55,000 graduate posts in 2017, vacancies are down 85pc.
summary: University graduates are facing the worst job market on record as vacancies drop significantly due to rising taxes, minimum wage increases, and the adoption of AI software. In July, only 8,383 graduate roles were advertised, representing a 45 percent decrease from the previous year. This downturn coincides with a record number of 18-year-olds preparing to start their degrees, while average graduate salaries have fallen to levels comparable to a full-time minimum wage job.
key_points: Graduate job vacancies dropped by 45 percent in July compared to the previous year, reaching the lowest level since records began in 2016.
Employers have reduced entry-level hiring following increases to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage.
Large employers are increasingly utilizing AI software to handle tasks traditionally assigned to graduates.
The average advertised graduate salary last month was £25,813, matching a full-time minimum wage income.

title: Shein aims for almost $27bn valuation in stock market debut
author: Osmond Chia
content:
![A woman in a red dress looks at her smartphone while walking past a Shein sign outside the company's office in Guangzhou, China.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/932/cpsprodpb/e462/live/c906d120-9f60-11f1-8564-6b99aa01bb8b.jpg)
- Published
Fast-fashion giant Shein says it plans to raise up to HK13.86bn (Â£1.3bn; $1.77bn) when its shares start trading on the Hong Kong stock market on 1 September.
In a filing on Monday, external, Shein said it will offer nearly 280 million shares for between HK$47.60 and HK$49.50.
At the top of the range, it would value the firm at almost $27bn (Â£19.8bn). But that is much lower than the $100bn valuation it reached in a round of private fundraising in 2022, reflecting weaker sales growth and higher costs.
The long-awaited move comes after failed attempts to list in the US and London due to regulatory challenges amid scrutiny of Shein, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China.
The initial public offering (IPO) is being backed by Wall Street investment giants Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan.
The company will make its highly anticipated debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after efforts to go public since 2023.
Hong Kong has been revived as "one of the largest IPO markets" after attracting more firms from mainland China, said economics associate professor Feng Qu from the Nanyang Technological University.
Shein is likely to command a higher valuation in Hong Kong than it would in London, where regulatory scrutiny derailed its plans to sell shares there, Feng said.
Chinese companies may also be wary of selling shares in the US as tensions between the world's two largest economies could result in firms being de-listed, he added.
Competition and roadblocks
Shein's listing will test investor confidence in the fast-fashion industry and its position in an increasingly competitive market.
In July, Shein said it had swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty waiver on small packages called the de minimis exemption.
The company said it lost $99m in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier.
It also came as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused.
"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said at the time.
The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets.
The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing.
Some investors are questioning whether higher costs and regulatory challenges will impact Shein's ability to get goods swiftly and cheaply to market.
Marguerite LeRolland from market research company Euromonitor International told the BBC that the firm's sales have slowed in the US partly due to the end of the de minimis exemption.
The exemption helped retailers like Shein and its fierce rival Temu grow quickly in the US as they were able to deliver goods without incurring import taxes.
These factors could "narrow the price gap" between Shein and competitors like Primark and H&M, she added.
![Workers producing garments at a Guangzhou textile factory that supplies clothes to Shein.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/69d4/live/0c9ef4d0-9f75-11f1-8f30-09408bc2783a.jpg)
Shein's fast-fashion clothes are backed by a network of factories in China
Since it was founded in 2008, Shein has risen to become one of the world's biggest fast-fashion retailers, with customers in more than 150 countries.
The e-commerce giant is known for selling ultra-cheap clothes, backed by a vast network of factories in China that are able to quickly manufacture new products based on the latest trends.
Its revenue has far outstripped rivals like H&M and Zara.
As of the end of March 2026 Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders.
But Shein's fast-fashion business has faced concerns over its environmental impact, and allegations of forced labour in supply chains. Shein has previously told the BBC it has a "zero tolerance for forced labour".
Its attempt to go public on the London Stock Exchange collapsed after the company came under scrutiny over its refusal to answer questions about its supply chain practices.
summary: Fast-fashion giant Shein plans to raise up to $1.77bn in a Hong Kong stock market debut on September 1, aiming for a valuation of almost $27bn. This expected valuation is significantly lower than the $100bn achieved in a 2022 private fundraising round, reflecting slower sales growth, higher costs, and regulatory challenges. The initial public offering follows failed attempts to list in the US and London.
key_points: Shein is offering nearly 280 million shares to raise up to HK$13.86bn ($1.77bn) on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
The target valuation of nearly $27bn is a major drop from its $100bn valuation in 2022 due to weaker sales and increased costs.
The listing follows abandoned IPO efforts in the US and London caused by regulatory scrutiny and geopolitical tensions.
Shein recently reported a quarterly loss driven by slowing US sales after the removal of the de minimis import duty exemption.
The company faces ongoing challenges regarding higher costs, delivery delays, environmental concerns, and supply chain scrutiny.

title: Why nearly 3 million Teslas are being recalled in China
author: Osmond Chia
content:
![A customer inspects the minimalistic hidden door handles on an electric car in a showroom.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/970/cpsprodpb/0e1b/live/441b98f0-9f52-11f1-8ce1-5fe0b29a148d.jpg)
Minimalistic hidden door handles have been a common feature in new electric cars
- Published
Minimalist retractable door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles.
The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations.
Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely.
Made popular by multi-billionaire Elon Musk's Tesla, hidden door handles are designed to tuck seamlessly within the car's door panel and only extend outwards approaches their vehicle.
The design came under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened.
Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are "difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim".
This could hinder occupants or rescuers from quickly opening the doors in an emergency, such as during a "severe collision causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail."
Tesla said it will place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle's windows after a collision.
It is not clear if the affected firms plan to make a similar recall for the rest of the world.
The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment.
In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles.
Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors.
Tesla's door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars.
In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers.
The BBC has contacted the agency for comment.
summary: China has initiated a massive vehicle recall affecting over 4 million cars, including nearly 3 million Teslas, due to safety concerns regarding minimalist hidden door handles. The design has faced scrutiny following crashes where power failures allegedly prevented doors from being opened during emergencies. In response, Chinese authorities have announced a ban on hidden door handles starting in 2027, requiring mechanical releases on all car doors.
key_points: More than 4 million vehicles are affected by China's largest car recall, including 2.98 million Teslas, as well as cars from XPeng, Xiaomi, and Geely.
The recall was prompted by concerns that hidden door handles are hard to locate and operate during emergencies, particularly after fatal crashes involving Xiaomi EVs with suspected power failures.
Tesla plans to address the issue by adding warning labels and issuing a software update to automatically lower vehicle windows after a collision.
China has announced a ban on hidden door handles, requiring all cars sold in the country to have mechanical releases on both the inside and outside of doors starting January 1, 2027.
Tesla's door handles have also faced scrutiny in the United States, where safety regulators investigated reports of them suddenly failing and trapping children inside.

title: UK productivity growing faster than official figures suggest, thinktank finds
author: Heather Stewart
content:
Productivity in the UK – a vital measure of economic health – is growing more strongly than official figures suggest, according to analysis from the Resolution Foundation.
The thinktank suggests the chancellor, John Healey, may have inherited an economy finally starting to emerge from the long shadow of the 2008 global financial crisis.
Productivity measures the economic output produced by each worker, and is a crucial determinant of growth.
The Resolution Foundation reconsiders the UK’s recent productivity record, using what it argues is a more accurate snapshot of the workforce than the widely criticised labour force survey.
Simon Pittaway, the thinktank’s principal economist, said: “Britain’s dismal productivity record since the global financial crisis explains a lot of its economic stagnation and weak living standards growth.
“But while official figures suggest that the output of workers has worsened further in the mid-2020s, our more accurate productivity measure suggests that it has been improving in recent years.”
Some economists have argued the potential uptick in productivity has resulted from job cuts in relatively low-skilled sectors such as hospitality and retail, meaning the average worker has become more productive.
However, the thinktank rejects that idea, pointing out that the share of the workforce employed in hospitality is no lower now than it was in the late 2010s, and only just below its post-pandemic peak.
It also suggests the uptick cannot just be AI-related, as it is more widespread across different sectors of the UK economy.
Pittaway said: “Some have suggested that recent productivity gains have been driven by an early AI boom, and workers leaving low-productivity sectors like retail and hospitality. But nether explanation is borne out by the data. Instead, the UK’s productivity recovery has been achieved by the same workers, doing the same jobs, and working in the same sectors.”
after newsletter promotion
The Resolution Foundation’s report was the latest to paint a relatively optimistic picture of the economy, after official figures last week showed the UK was the joint fastest-growing economy in the G7 in the first half of 2026.
John Van Reenen, Rachel Reeves’s former chief economic adviser, recently published a blogpost pointing to a similar productivity rethink by him and his colleagues at the London School of Economics.
Economists at Morgan Stanley said in a recent research note that the UK was now in “an OK place”. In a note titled “The vibes they are a-changin’”, its chief UK economist, Bruna Skarica, pointed out that growth and inflation had been hit less hard than feared by the Iran war, and consumer confidence had reached a two-year high.
summary: According to an analysis by the Resolution Foundation, UK productivity is growing faster than official figures indicate, suggesting the economy is emerging from the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The thinktank used a more accurate workforce snapshot to conclude that productivity has improved in recent years. This recovery is driven by workers across the same jobs and sectors, rather than being solely the result of artificial intelligence or job cuts in low-skilled industries.
key_points: The Resolution Foundation reports that UK productivity growth is stronger than official statistics show.
The thinktank's analysis relies on a more accurate snapshot of the workforce than the labour force survey.
Data refutes the claims that recent productivity gains stem from an AI boom or job cuts in low-skilled sectors like hospitality and retail.
Other economic reports similarly show positive trends, including the UK being the joint fastest-growing G7 economy in the first half of 2026.

title: Review launched into how pub and hotel business rates calculated
author: Nick Edser
content:
![A man wearing a blue top pouring a pint in a pub](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/7f38/live/0b0cedf0-9ed7-11f1-9253-c70a43a5293b.jpg)
- Published
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.
The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.
Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.
Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.
According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.
Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.
James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".
Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."
The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.
Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.
His appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".
However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.
Tom Ironside from the British Retail Consortium also welcomed the review but said it was "vitally important that the needs of retailers are not overlooked".
Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".
"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.
Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".
Last year, under the previous chancellor Rachel Reeves, the government had said it would scale back business rate discounts that had been in force since the Covid pandemic and announced that there would be no discount at all from April this year.
That, combined with big upward adjustments to rateable values of pub premises, left landlords with the prospect of much higher bills.
Following criticism from the hospitality industry, the government cut business rates for pubs and music venues by 15% earlier in 2026.
The 20% discount in England announced in July will apply on top of the existing support.
However, the government said the rates discount would not apply to the "very largest" live music venues, and there was some confusion among some businesses as to whether they would be classed as a pub and therefore eligible for the relief.
Details about which businesses are eligible are expected to be announced at Chancellor John Healey's first Budget in the autumn.
summary: The UK government has launched a review into how business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales. Led by expert Jerry Schurder, the review will examine rate valuations and report back in March 2027 to feed into the 2029 revaluation. Industry groups welcomed the initiative, citing disproportionately high rates for pubs, though other business sectors called for broader system reforms and relief.
key_points: A government review led by Jerry Schurder will examine business rates valuations for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, reporting back in March 2027.
Pubs are currently valued using Fair Maintainable Trade, meaning their rates increase alongside their turnover rather than solely based on floor area.
The British Beer and Pub Association welcomed the review, stating that pubs have long paid disproportionately higher business rates.
Other groups, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the British Retail Consortium, emphasized the need for wider system reforms and consideration for smaller firms and retailers.
The review follows recent government announcements of business rate cuts and discounts for pubs, social clubs, and live music venues.

title: The Treasury's recent moves in the bond and currency markets add up to 'soft-form financial repression' to lower debt costs, economist warns | Fortune
author: Jason Ma
content:
With U.S. debt hitting $40 trillion, markets are turning more attention to that burden and whether policymakers will address the root causes or just the symptoms.
The Treasury Department’s interventions in the bond and currency markets in recent weeks point to the latter.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent surprised Wall Street on Wednesday with a plan to increase buybacks of long-term bonds, after the 30-year yield hit the highest level in nearly 20 years.
That came just a few weeks after the U.S. and Japan took such joint action to boost the yen for the first time in three decades. But to make it happen, the U.S. sold euros instead of dollar-denominated assets, avoiding a sale of Treasury securities that would put more upward pressure on yields.
Japan also refrained from selling Treasuries and instead tapped an obscure Federal Reserve tool called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility (FIMA). This mechanism allowed Japan, which is the world’s largest holder of U.S. debt, to borrow dollars against its Treasury stockpile, obtaining a limited form of liquidity.
According to George Saravelos, head of FX research at Deutsche Bank, “we see both the buyback and encouragement to use the FIMA facility for FX reserves as soft-form financial repression policies aimed at containing the long-end of the US yield curve.”
Financial repression generally refers to policies that enable a government to keep interest rates artificially low by influencing financial markets.
Countries throughout history have practiced it, especially during times of high indebtedness. In fact, the U.S. and other developed economies used financial repression to slash their debt-to-GDP ratios after World War II.
Indeed, conflict and calamities are major factors in financial repression. A recent survey of 300 years of U.S. and U.K. history found that wars are “always disaster times” for holders of government debt because of inflation and financial repression.
It’s not good for currencies either. Saravelos warned that suppressing U.S. Treasury yields will merely shift the impact to the dollar.
“If the market price of USTs is not ‘allowed’ to adjust down, the foreign exchange price of UST owned by foreign investors has to adjust via a weakening in the dollar,” he explained.
Markets will next scrutinize how the Federal Reserve responds, Saravelos predicted, pointing out that Bessent’s moves to effectively loosen financial conditions would typically prompt the Fed to offset that with tightening measures.
That’s as the Fed has been especially wary of inflation, which has exceeded its 2% target for more than five years, with several central bankers ready to hike rates. But Chairman Kevin Warsh has refrained from so-called forward guidance, leaving Wall Street guessing on his stance.
“If Chair Warsh does not recognize the buyback as a factor driving an easing of financial conditions, we would take it as an additional dollar negative driver,” Saravelos added. “In all, the market is likely to be increasingly attentive to further measures intended to support the US Treasury market going forward. The more these are perceived as distortionary to market pricing, the more the dollar is likely to weaken.”
Since the debt buyback was unveiled, markets have ramped up bets on the “debasement trade,” with prices for gold and bitcoin surging on expectations of further dollar devaluation.
That’s because the root causes of the recent jump in bond yields—especially massive debt and deficits—are not priorities among most lawmakers.
The federal budget deficit is on track to hit $2 trillion this fiscal year, and debt interest costs alone are already $1 trillion annually, taking up a bigger and bigger share of spending. But there’s no sign Washington is serious about slashing the budget or raising taxes.
Absent such moves, the solution to higher borrowing costs is likely more repression. A research paper last month from the International Monetary Fund said the world is ripe for another wave.
“With the conditions historically associated with elevated repression present today, our evidence suggests that financial repression may see increased use going forward,” it said.
summary: As U.S. debt reaches $40 trillion and budget deficits climb toward $2 trillion, the Treasury Department is implementing interventions in bond and currency markets to lower debt costs. Economist George Saravelos warns that these actions amount to 'soft-form financial repression' designed to artificially contain long-term yields. While these measures aim to manage borrowing expenses without addressing root fiscal causes, experts note they risk weakening the U.S. dollar and driving up assets like gold and bitcoin.
key_points: U.S. debt has reached $40 trillion, with annual interest costs exceeding $1 trillion and budget deficits heading toward $2 trillion.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a plan to increase long-term bond buybacks after 30-year yields hit nearly 20-year highs.
Recent U.S. and Japanese currency interventions avoided selling U.S. Treasuries by utilizing Euro sales and the Fed's FIMA repo facility.
Deutsche Bank's George Saravelos warns that suppressing Treasury yields constitutes 'soft-form financial repression' that could weaken the U.S. dollar.
Prices for gold and bitcoin have surged on expectations of dollar devaluation as markets react to the Treasury's market interventions.

title: All you need to know as south Essex to be hit by 6 DAYS of train disruption
author: Matthew Benton-Smith
content:
Passengers using c2c services across south Essex are being warned of late-evening cancellations, diversions and replacement shuttle arrangements throughout the week due to engineering works.
The disruption will affect services on the Basildon, Ockendon and Rainham lines between August 24 and August 29.
Separate works at Limehouse mean London-bound c2c trains will not call at the station until August 29.
Monday, August 24
Engineering work between Fenchurch Street and Barking from around 8.45pm, followed by work between Barking and Upminster from around 10.45pm, will affect several routes.
On the Basildon line, services from around 8.45pm will be diverted to Liverpool Street via Stratford, meaning they will not call at Limehouse or West Ham.
The final Fenchurch Street to Shoeburyness service via Basildon will leave at 8.29pm, running fast from Pitsea to Shoeburyness.
From around 10.45pm, Basildon line services will be diverted via Grays and will not call at Upminster, West Horndon, Laindon or Basildon.
Shuttle trains will operate between Upminster and Pitsea via Laindon.
The final Liverpool Street to Shoeburyness service via Basildon will leave at 9.52pm.
On the Ockendon line, trains will operate as shuttles between Upminster and Grays.
The final Fenchurch Street to Shoeburyness service via Ockendon will leave at 8.11pm.
On the Rainham line, trains from around 8.45pm will be diverted to Liverpool Street via Stratford and will not stop at Limehouse or West Ham.
Services will be extended to Southend Central or Shoeburyness.
The final Fenchurch Street to Grays service via Rainham will leave at 8.23pm.
Tuesday, August 25
The same evening engineering works will be in place, with temporary speed restrictions also affecting c2c services all day.
On the Basildon line, services from around 8.45pm will be diverted to Liverpool Street via Stratford, not calling at Limehouse or West Ham.
The final Fenchurch Street to Shoeburyness service via Basildon will leave at 8.19pm and will not stop at West Horndon or Pitsea.
After around 10.45pm, services will be diverted via Grays, missing Upminster, West Horndon, Laindon and Basildon.
Shuttle trains will run between Upminster and Pitsea via Laindon.
The final Liverpool Street to Shoeburyness service via Basildon will leave at 9.52pm.
The Ockendon line will again run only as a shuttle between Upminster and Grays.
The final Fenchurch Street to Shoeburyness service via Ockendon will leave at 8.11pm.
On the Rainham line, services from around 8.45pm will be diverted to Liverpool Street via Stratford, will not call at Limehouse or West Ham, and will continue to Southend Central or Shoeburyness.
The final Fenchurch Street to Grays service via Rainham will leave at 8.23pm.
Wednesday, August 26
The same restrictions and engineering arrangements as Tuesday will remain in place.
Temporary speed restrictions will affect services throughout the day, with passengers urged to check before travelling.
From around 8.45pm, Basildon and Rainham line services will be diverted to Liverpool Street via Stratford, missing Limehouse and West Ham.
Ockendon line services will operate only between Upminster and Grays.
After around 10.45pm, Basildon line services will run via Grays and will not call at Upminster, West Horndon, Laindon or Basildon.
Shuttles will run between Upminster and Pitsea via Laindon.
The final Fenchurch Street to Shoeburyness service via Basildon leaves at 8.19pm and will not stop at West Horndon or Pitsea.
The final Ockendon service leaves at 8.11pm, while the final Fenchurch Street to Grays service via Rainham leaves at 8.23pm.
